context: HackTricks Linux Privilege Escalation guide section on kernel-exploit enumeration: covers uname/proc-version checks, searchsploit queries, the lucyoa/kernel-exploits compiled-exploit repository, and helper scripts linux-exploit-suggester(.sh/.pl) and linuxprivchecker.py for identifying vulnerable Linux kernel versions on a target host.

HackTricks Linux privesc section on the sudo chroot vulnerability CVE-2025-32463 affecting Sudo 1.9.14-1.9.17 before 1.9.17p1, where the --chroot option lets an unprivileged user load a malicious /etc/nsswitch.conf from a controlled directory to gain root. References pr0v3rbs PoC.

HackTricks Linux privesc coverage of CVE-2025-32462, a Sudo host-based-rules bypass in versions 1.8.8 to 1.9.17 before 1.9.17p1 where sudo -h <host> evaluates user-supplied hostname against sudoers Host_Alias entries, enabling local hostname spoofing to gain privileges granted on other hosts.

HackTricks Linux privesc enumeration of drives and mounts: inspecting /dev, /etc/fstab, and /etc/mtab for unmounted volumes and embedded credentials (user/password/login fields) as part of post-exploitation host triage.

HackTricks Linux privesc enumeration of useful binaries on a target (nmap, nc, netcat, socat, gcc, python, docker, kubectl, etc.) and compilers, plus identifying installed software for offline-host exploit compilation when no compiler is present.

HackTricks Linux privesc step on enumerating vulnerable installed package versions via dpkg -l and rpm -qa, plus openVAS-style host-vuln scanning to find outdated services such as Nagios that can be leveraged for local privilege escalation.

HackTricks Linux privesc enumeration of running processes via ps aux / ps -ef / top, looking for over-privileged services (e.g., Tomcat-as-root) and Electron/CEF/Chromium debugger ports that linpeas flags for potential abuse.

HackTricks Linux privesc technique on detecting cross-user parent-child process chains as a triage signal for wrappers, debug helpers, persistence and weak runtime trust boundaries that may enable privilege escalation on Linux hosts.

HackTricks Linux privesc technique on recovering deleted-but-still-open executables and files via /proc/$pid/exe and /proc/$pid/fd, useful for both privesc and forensic recovery of sensitive data held by running processes.

HackTricks Linux privesc section on harvesting clear-text credentials from process memory, noting root is normally required to read other users' process memory while regular users can read their own processes' memory.

HackTricks Linux privesc deep-dive on /proc/$pid/maps and /proc/$pid/mem for reading a process's virtual memory regions, identifying readable mappings and offsets to dump sensitive secrets stored in memory.

HackTricks Linux privesc walkthrough of ProcDump-for-Linux (Sysinternals port) for dumping a target process's memory to disk for offline credential extraction during local privilege-escalation workflows.

HackTricks Linux privesc reference list of process-memory-dumping tools: ProcDump-for-Linux, hajzer/bash-memory-dump, and Nelson Elhage's Script A.5 for extracting process memory without requiring root in some cases.
HackTricks Linux privesc manual example of dumping an 'authenticator' process's memory and grepping the dump for clear-text credentials to escalate via reused passwords found in RAM.

HackTricks Linux privesc coverage of mimipenguin (huntergregal/mimipenguin), a Mimikatz-equivalent for Linux that scrapes clear-text credentials from gdm/vsftpd/sshd/Apache process memory and well-known files (requires root).

HackTricks Linux privesc technique abusing alseambusher/crontab-ui running as root and bound to loopback: reach the web panel via SSH local port-forwarding and create a privileged cron job to escalate to root.

HackTricks Linux privesc follow-up to the Crontab UI privesc chain: payload cp /bin/bash /tmp/rootshell && chmod 6777 to produce a SUID root shell, plus hardening guidance (do not run Crontab UI as root, bind to localhost, no secret reuse).

HackTricks Linux privesc abuse of writable directories in the cron PATH variable: when /etc/crontab sets PATH=/home/user:... and root runs an unqualified command, an attacker drops a same-named binary into the writable PATH entry to gain root execution.

HackTricks Linux privesc wildcard-injection technique against root cron jobs that use unquoted globs (e.g., rsync -a *.sh), exploiting filename-as-option tricks like '-e sh myscript.sh' to inject commands that execute as root.

HackTricks Linux privesc Bash arithmetic-expansion injection in cron log parsers: untrusted log fields feeding into ((...)), $((...)) or let undergo parameter expansion and command substitution $(...) before evaluation, yielding root code execution.

HackTricks Linux privesc abuse of writable cron scripts run as root: overwrite the script with 'cp /bin/bash /tmp/bash; chmod +s /tmp/bash' to obtain a SUID root bash, and related write-to-script-directory and symlink-swap variants.

HackTricks Linux privesc reference on symlink validation in privileged scripts: stat() vs lstat() behavior, readlink -f and namei -l for resolving link targets, and safer file handling patterns to avoid TOCTOU/symlink-swap exploitation.

HackTricks Linux privesc trick for custom-signed cron binaries: when a group-writable root-cron binary (e.g., /opt/AV/periodic-checks/monitor mode 770) is 'signed' via a custom ELF section, forging the .text_sig section after leaking signing material lets you hijack execution as root (HTB Era reference).

HackTricks Linux privesc technique using pspy-style process monitoring (or a shell for-loop ps snapshot) to discover frequent cron jobs running every 1/2/5 minutes that may be exploitable for privilege escalation.

HackTricks Linux privesc abuse of root cron jobs wrapping pg_basebackup against an attacker-writable database directory: planting a SUID/SGID binary whose mode bits are preserved during backup yields a root-owned setuid binary in the backup output.

HackTricks Linux privesc follow-up on pg_basebackup-as-root abuse: confirming /opt/backups/current/bash gets mode -rwsrwsrwx after the backup run, then invoking it with -p to drop into a root shell without dropping privileges.

HackTricks Linux privesc stealth technique of 'invisible cron jobs': inserting a carriage-return after a comment in a crontab so the trailing entry still runs but is hidden in casual review; detection guidance for blue teams included.

HackTricks Linux privesc abuse of writable systemd .service unit files: modify ExecStart/ExecStop to point at an attacker-controlled backdoor that runs as root when the service starts, restarts, or the host reboots.

HackTricks Linux privesc trick exploiting systemd PATH with relative ExecStart paths: if any folder in systemctl show-environment PATH is writable and a unit uses a relative binary name, drop a malicious binary there for root execution.
HackTricks Linux privesc coverage of systemd .timer units (calendar and monotonic time events) as a cron alternative, enumerating timers as part of privesc reconnaissance.

HackTricks Linux privesc abuse of writable systemd .timer units: modify the Unit= directive so an attacker-controlled backdoor.service is activated when the timer elapses, granting root code execution.

HackTricks Linux privesc note on enabling systemd timers via 'systemctl enable backu2.timer' (which symlinks into /etc/systemd/system/<target>.wants/), highlighting writable-symlink-path vectors for privesc.

HackTricks Linux privesc introduction to Unix Domain Sockets (UDS) and .socket unit files for inter-process communication, framing later abuse of writable .socket files and Docker socket for privilege escalation.

HackTricks Linux privesc abuse of writable systemd .socket files: insert ExecStartPre=/home/kali/sys/backdoor in the [Socket] section so the backdoor executes before the socket is created on next boot or reload.

HackTricks Linux privesc technique on systemd socket activation with missing-service abuse: when Accept=no and Service=<name>.service points to an absent unit, an attacker writes the missing service into /etc/systemd/system to achieve root code execution.

HackTricks Linux privesc reference on raw Unix-socket connection tooling: nc -U / nc -uU for stream/datagram sockets and socat UNIX-CLIENT for type-agnostic connections, used during socket-command-injection exploitation.

HackTricks Linux privesc technique for HTTP-over-Unix-socket targets: probing with curl --unix-socket /path/to/socket http://localhost/ to detect HTTP-speaking sockets that may expose privileged APIs.

HackTricks Linux privesc abuse of writable Docker socket /var/run/docker.sock: any user in the docker group or with write access to the socket can escalate to root, with multiple exploitation paths covered.

HackTricks Linux privesc Docker-socket abuse via Docker CLI: 'docker run -v /:/host -it ubuntu chroot /host /bin/bash' and 'docker run --privileged --pid=host debian nsenter -t 1 -m -u -n -i sh' for root on the host.

HackTricks Linux privesc Docker-socket abuse using raw Docker API via curl --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock when the docker CLI is unavailable: listing images, creating privileged containers, and starting them to mount host root.
HackTricks Linux privesc note that docker-group membership provides additional privesc paths and that exposed Docker API on TCP 2375 (port 2375 pentesting page) can also be leveraged for compromise.
HackTricks Linux privesc introduction to D-Bus IPC: describing system and session buses as a target for privilege escalation via misconfigured policy and service exposure on modern Linux hosts.

HackTricks Linux privesc generic network enumeration: reading /etc/hostname, /etc/hosts, /etc/resolv.conf, nsswitch.conf, /etc/inetd.conf, /etc/xinetd.conf and interface info (ifconfig/ip a) for host-network triage.

HackTricks Linux privesc open-port enumeration on the local host with netstat -punta, ss -tulpn, and grep 127.0 for loopback-bound services that were unreachable pre-foothold (proxy-enforced/remote-DNS SOCKS scenarios).

HackTricks Linux privesc traffic-sniffing checks: tcpdump with caps via getcap on dumpcap, listing capture interfaces (tcpdump -D), and the value of loopback (lo) sniffing during post-exploitation for IPC and loopback-only services.
HackTricks Linux privesc generic user enumeration: id/whoami/groups, /etc/passwd parsing for console users and superusers (UID 0), enumerating login-capable accounts for further targeting.

HackTricks Linux privesc reference to CVE-2018-19788, the polkit Big-UID bug where users with UID > INT_MAX can escalate privileges on affected Linux systems; links to mirchr PoC and freedesktop polkit issue 74.
HackTricks Linux privesc clipboard-content harvesting via xclip and xsel for selection/clipboard secrets that may include credentials pasted by other desktop users.
HackTricks Linux privesc noisy brute-force option using carlospolop/su-bruteforce and linpeas -a flag to bruteforce su passwords for other local users when stealth is not a concern.

HackTricks Linux privesc writable-PATH abuse: when a $PATH directory is user-writable and earlier in the search order than the legitimate command's location, planting a same-named backdoor binary yields execution as the higher-privileged user.

HackTricks Linux privesc SUDO and SUID enumeration via 'sudo -l' and 'find / -perm -4000', framing the GTFOBins-style abuse of unexpected SUID/sudoers commands that allow file read/write or shell execution.
HackTricks Linux privesc NOPASSWD sudoers abuse: when 'sudo -l' shows '(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim', escape to a root shell via vim's :!sh or equivalent GTFOBins escape.

HackTricks Linux privesc abuse of sudo SETENV directive: HTB Admirer machine example exploiting PYTHONPATH hijacking through (ALL) SETENV: /opt/scripts/admin_tasks.sh to load an arbitrary Python module as root.

HackTricks Linux privesc technique: writable __pycache__ / .pyc poisoning against sudo-allowed Python scripts, replacing the cached bytecode of an imported module so CPython loads the attacker payload during the next privileged import.

HackTricks Linux privesc continuation of __pycache__/.pyc poisoning: concrete Python snippet that compiles a payload, prepends the correct magic header and marshals the code object into the writable .pyc, then invokes the sudo-allowed runner.

HackTricks Linux privesc trick using BASH_ENV preserved by sudo env_keep+=BASH_ENV: Bash sources $BASH_ENV in non-interactive shells, so a sudo-allowed bash-invoking command runs attacker code as root.

HackTricks Linux privesc Terraform-via-sudo abuse with !env_reset: $HOME stays as the caller so 'terraform apply' loads $HOME/.terraformrc and honors provider_installation.dev_overrides to load a malicious provider plugin as root.

HackTricks Linux privesc concrete Terraform dev_overrides payload: ~/.terraformrc points provider previous.htb/terraform/examples to /dev/shm, a shell script masquerading as terraform-provider-examples cp's /bin/bash and chmod 6777 it for a SUID root shell.

HackTricks Linux privesc Terraform TF_VAR override and symlink validation-bypass technique: TF_VAR_<name> survives sudo env preservation, and weak strcontains() path checks are bypassed by symlinking /root paths from /dev/shm.

HackTricks Linux privesc note on sudo requiretty / !requiretty: when !requiretty is set or absent, sudo can be invoked from non-interactive contexts like reverse shells, cron, or scripts during privesc chains.

HackTricks Linux privesc abuse of sudo env_keep+=PATH or insecure secure_path containing user-writable entries (e.g., /home/<user>/bin), allowing relative commands inside the sudo-allowed target script to be shadowed by attacker binaries.
HackTricks Linux privesc 'sudo less' GTFOBins escape: when sudoers allows /bin/less /var/log/*, use :e /etc/shadow inside less or symlink /etc/shadow into /var/log to read arbitrary root-owned files.

HackTricks Linux privesc abuse of sudo rules without absolute command paths (e.g., 'hacker10 ALL=(root) less'): prepend a writable directory to PATH and place a malicious 'less' binary to execute as root.

HackTricks Linux privesc bash function-export trick against SUID binaries calling absolute-path subcommands: export -f a function named 'apache2' (when the SUID runs /usr/sbin/service apache2 start) to hijack execution as root.

HackTricks Linux privesc pattern of a root-owned SUID C wrapper that system()'s a user-writable shell script (/usr/local/bin/backup.sh): overwriting the writable script content yields root code execution when the wrapper is run.

HackTricks Linux privesc LD_PRELOAD and LD_LIBRARY_PATH abuse: dynamic-loader env vars that preload a .so before libc, blocked by default for SUID/SGID unless sudoers env_keep preserves them, enabling code execution as the target user.

HackTricks Linux privesc SUID .so injection technique: strace the SUID binary for failed open()/access() on shared libraries (e.g., libcalc.so) in user-writable paths, then compile and place a malicious .so there to gain root.

HackTricks Linux privesc SUID-with-RUNPATH abuse: 'readelf -d payroll | grep PATH' reveals a writable RUNPATH like /development; compile libshared.so via gcc -fPIC -shared into that directory to hijack the SUID binary's library loading.

HackTricks Linux privesc reference to GTFOBins and GTFOArgs: curated lists of Unix binaries whose legitimate functionality (read/write/shell/sudo) can be abused to bypass local security restrictions when allowed via sudo or available as SUID.

HackTricks Linux privesc sudo-token reuse: when sampleuser has used sudo in the last 15 minutes and you have a shell as them, hijack the cached sudo session token (in /var/run/sudo/ts/) to run sudo without knowing the password.

HackTricks Linux privesc tooling for forging sudo tokens: nongiach/sudo_inject's write_sudo_token binary creates a sudo timestamp file in /var/run/sudo/ts/<Username> for a chosen PID, granting passwordless sudo on the next invocation.

HackTricks Linux privesc treatment of /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d: reading these (default root:root only) reveals exploitable rules, and writing to them grants arbitrary sudo privileges for any user.

HackTricks Linux privesc sudo-hijacking persistence: drop a fake 'sudo' binary in a PATH directory loaded before /usr/bin via .bash_profile, then capture the password and proxy to real sudo the next time the target user runs it. Also notes DOAS as an alternative target.

HackTricks Linux privesc shared-library hijacking via /etc/ld.so.conf and ld.so.conf.d: writable include paths let an attacker prepend a malicious library directory so libc lookups load attacker .so files into privileged binaries.
HackTricks Linux privesc Nebula level15 RPATH exploitation walkthrough: a SUID binary has RPATH=/var/tmp/flag15, allowing the attacker to place a malicious libc.so.6 there for hijacked execution.

HackTricks Linux privesc introduction to Linux capabilities (POSIX caps): file and process capabilities partition root power into units like cap_setuid, cap_dac_read_search, cap_sys_admin that can each be abused for privesc when granted to user-controllable binaries.
HackTricks Linux privesc coverage of POSIX ACLs (getfacl/setfacl) as a secondary permission layer overriding ugo/rwx, enabling unexpected file access that bypasses traditional permission triage.

HackTricks Linux privesc hidden-ACL backdoor on /etc/sudoers.d/ drop-ins: a mode-440 root-owned file with an ACL user:alice:rw- lets alice append her own NOPASSWD sudo rule despite restrictive Unix permission bits.

HackTricks Linux privesc tmux session hijacking: list tmux sessions and sockets (tmux ls, ps aux | grep tmux, tmux -S /tmp/dev_sess ls) to attach to a root tmux session created with a world-readable socket path.

HackTricks Linux privesc reference to CVE-2008-0166, the Debian OpenSSL Predictable PRNG vulnerability: SSH/SSL keys generated on Debian/Ubuntu between Sept 2006 and May 2008 are drawn from only 32,768 variants, enabling offline brute-force of all possible keys.

HackTricks Linux privesc rundown of SSH server config values: PasswordAuthentication, PubkeyAuthentication, PermitEmptyPasswords and related sshd_config directives relevant during host hardening review.

HackTricks Linux privesc breakdown of sshd PermitRootLogin values: yes / without-password (prohibit-password) / forced-commands-only / no, and what each means for remote root access during privesc evaluation.
HackTricks Linux privesc explanation of sshd AuthorizedKeysFile directive (with %h token expansion), and the implication of writable authorized_keys paths for persistence and pivoting.

HackTricks Linux privesc SSH agent-forwarding (ForwardAgent / AllowAgentForwarding) abuse: when a target host has access to your forwarded agent, an attacker with root on that host can use the socket to authenticate to other systems.
HackTricks Linux privesc abuse of /etc/profile and /etc/profile.d/ login scripts: writable entries get executed for every new login shell, providing a path to root or persistence when modifiable.
HackTricks Linux privesc enumeration of /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and their backup variants (passwd-, shadow-, master.passwd, /etc/pwd.db) to find readable password hashes for offline cracking.
HackTricks Linux privesc writable /etc/passwd attack: generate a SHA-512 hash with openssl passwd/mkpasswd/python crypt and append a hacker:HASH:0:0::/root:/bin/bash line to gain a UID-0 account.

HackTricks Linux privesc enumeration of weird-location / weird-owner files: find root-owned files in /home, files owned by other users in directories owned by you, and other anomalies that may signal privesc opportunities.

HackTricks Linux privesc find-command for credential-containing files: *_history, .sudo_as_admin_successful, .profile, *bashrc, httpd.conf, .plan, .htpasswd, .git-credentials, .rhosts, hosts.equiv, Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml across the filesystem.
HackTricks Linux privesc reference to linPEAS and LaZagne (Alessandro Z) for automated discovery of password-bearing files across the filesystem during local privilege-escalation enumeration.

HackTricks Linux privesc abuse of readable logs and audit logs: misconfigured/backdoored audit subsystems may log passwords typed at the TTY, yielding plaintext credentials to any user able to read the audit log.

HackTricks Linux privesc reference to Bash startup-file ordering: ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.profile, /etc/profile and ~/.bashrc, useful both for finding stored secrets and for implanting persistence on writable startup files.

HackTricks Linux privesc generic credential search: grep filenames and contents for 'password', email addresses, IPs and known hash regexes; linpeas's final checks are referenced as a template for automated credential mining.

HackTricks Linux privesc Python library hijacking: if you can write to a directory in the Python import path used by a privileged script, drop a backdoored os.py (or similar module) to gain code execution as the privileged user.

HackTricks Linux privesc logrotate exploitation: writable log files or directories let an attacker abuse logrotate (running as root) to execute arbitrary files, often through /etc/bash_completion.d/ for root code execution.

HackTricks Linux privesc CentOS/RedHat-specific abuse of writable /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-* files: NAME= field values get shell-evaluated by network-scripts, yielding root code execution (vulmon disclosure referenced).

HackTricks Linux privesc abuse of SysVinit /etc/init.d, /etc/rc?.d/ symlinks, systemd unit files and rc.d on BSD-like systems: writable init scripts run as root at service start, restart, or boot, granting persistence and escalation.

HackTricks Linux privesc Android rooting-framework manager-channel abuse: weak manager authentication (FD-order based signature checks, weak password schemes) lets a local Android app impersonate the manager and obtain root on already-rooted devices.

HackTricks Linux privesc coverage of CVE-2025-41244, a VMware Tools / Aria Operations local privilege escalation (CWE-426) where regex-based service discovery using permissive \S patterns matches attacker-staged binaries in writable paths and executes them with -v under a privileged context.
HackTricks Linux privesc tooling roundup: LinPEAS (carlospolop), LinEnum -t (rebootuser), Enumy (luke-goddard) and related automated Linux local privilege-escalation enumeration scripts.

HackTricks Linux privesc references section linking 0xdf writeups for HTB Planning (Crontab UI privesc, zip -P credential reuse), HTB Era (forged .text_sig payload for cron-executed monitor binary), and the Holiday Hack Challenge 2025 Neighborhood Watch sudo env_keep PATH-hijack bypass.

Overview section of the HackTricks page on AI-Assisted Fuzzing & Automated Vulnerability Discovery. Introduces LLM-driven vulnerability-research pipelines (semantic input generation, grammar evolution, crash reasoning, multi-bug patching) abstracted from DARPA AI Cyber Challenge (AIxCC) finals and public Cyber Reasoning System (CRS) research, framing the techniques covered in the rest of the document.

Section 1 (LLM-Generated Seed Inputs) of the HackTricks AI-Assisted Fuzzing page. Covers using LLMs to bootstrap coverage-guided fuzzers (AFL++, libFuzzer, Honggfuzz) on complex input formats like SQL by prompting the model to emit Python seed-generator scripts that print syntax-valid, security-relevant payloads (e.g. SQL injection strings) for the fuzzer corpus.

Continuation of Section 1 (LLM-Generated Seed Inputs) showing the gen_sqli_seeds.py SQLi payload list (OR 1=1, UNION SELECT NULL, stacked DROP TABLE) and the afl-fuzz invocation `afl-fuzz -i seeds.txt -o findings/ -- ./target @@` used to feed LLM-generated seeds into AFL, with benefits including semantic validity, prompt-retargeting for XSS/path traversal, and sub-cent GPT-3.5 cost.

Section 2 (Grammar-Evolution Fuzzing) of the HackTricks AI-Assisted Fuzzing page. Documents the "Grammar Guy" pattern: generate an initial ANTLR/Peach/LibFuzzer grammar via LLM prompt, fuzz, feed uncovered-function coverage stats back to the model to refine grammar rules iteratively, using diff/patch edits and stopping when delta-coverage falls below epsilon.

Section 3 (Agent-Based PoV / Exploit Generation) of the HackTricks AI-Assisted Fuzzing page. Describes spawning thousands of parallel LLM agents (GPT-4, Claude, Mixtral at varying temperatures) that consume bug-candidate structs (crash PC, input slice, sanitizer message), reproduce crashes under gdb, synthesize minimal exploit payloads, and validate in sandbox to produce deterministic proof-of-vulnerability artifacts.

Section 4 (Directed Fuzzing with Fine-Tuned Code Models) of the HackTricks AI-Assisted Fuzzing page. Covers fine-tuning open-weight models like Llama-7B on labelled C/C++ vulnerability patterns (integer overflow, buffer copy, format string) to emit mutation-dictionary entries (e.g. `%99999999s`, `%n` format-string payloads) loaded into AFL_CUSTOM_MUTATOR for >2x faster time-to-crash.

Section 5.1 (Super Patches) under AI-Guided Patching Strategies on the HackTricks AI-Assisted Fuzzing page. Describes prompting an LLM to cluster crash signatures across multiple stack traces and generate a single unified diff that removes the shared root cause, optimizing for AIxCC-style scoring where wrong patches incur accuracy penalties.

Final "Putting It All Together" section of the HackTricks AI-Assisted Fuzzing page. Presents a Mermaid graph wiring an end-to-end Cyber Reasoning System (CRS): LLM seed/grammar generation and fine-tuned mutation dictionaries feed a fuzzer, crashes flow into a crash DB, agent-based PoV generation produces exploits, and clustered crashes drive LLM super-patches into a patch submitter.

Covers the macOS variant of MITRE ATT&CK T1143 (Hidden Window), detailing abuse of the apple.awt.UIElement plist tag to suppress Java application Dock icons and hide running windows from users, citing Antiquated Mac Malware backdoor tradecraft.

Reference links for MITRE ATT&CK T1143 (Hidden Window), including the canonical attack.mitre.org technique page, Microsoft PowerShell.exe documentation, and the Malwarebytes Antiquated Mac Malware backdoor analysis cited for the macOS plist UIElement abuse.

Describes a Content-Type/CORB XS-Leak oracle using a script src inclusion. When an endpoint returns HTML on match versus JSON on mismatch, CORB blocks the JSON response and fires onerror, creating a Boolean oracle to brute-force identifiers such as __user without reading response bodies.

Describes a postMessage versus X-Frame-Options XS-Leak oracle using iframe inclusion. Describes the XS-Leak onload timing technique for cross-origin page state inference. Uses performance.now() and PerformanceLongTaskTiming API (tasks >50ms) as clocks to measure request duration via HTML element inclusion, leaking status code or page content differences through timing.

Describes the XS-Leak unload/beforeunload timing technique using frame inclusion. Measures time between beforeunload (navigation start) and unload (navigation occurring) events via SharedArrayBuffer clock to determine how long the browser spent fetching a cross-origin resource.

Describes the XS-Leak sandboxed iframe timing attack. Uses the sandbox attribute on iframes to suppress JavaScript execution, making performance.now() timing measurements reflect only network latency when loading cross-origin pages, allowing status code and page content inference without script interference.

Describes the XS-Leak #ID + error + onload technique for extracting cross-origin page content without timing. Uses an iframe with CSRF-triggered search; exploits the fact that onload re-fires on error but not on same-URL hash change, creating a Boolean oracle to brute-force secret content character by character.

Describes the XS-Leak JavaScript execution technique for cross-origin content leakage. If a page reflects user-controlled content, attacker pre-defines JavaScript code so it executes in negative (mismatch) cases when the page is loaded inside a script tag, and does not execute in positive (match) cases.

Describes the XS-Leak CORB onerror technique. Cross-Origin Read Blocking (CORB) strips body and headers from responses with a CORB-protected Content-Type, nosniff, and 2xx status; attackers observe whether onerror fires to infer the status code and Content-Type combination of a cross-origin resource.

Describes the XS-Leak onblur technique for leaking cross-origin element IDs. An iframe is loaded with a URL fragment targeting a specific element ID; if onblur fires, the element with that ID exists in the cross-origin page. The same attack works with portal tags as the inclusion method.

Describes the XS-Leak postMessage broadcasts technique. Cross-origin applications leaking sensitive data via postMessage without a strict targetOrigin allow any window to receive messages. References allanlw/svg-cheatsheet.

XSS payload and resource link collection. References PayloadsAllTheThings XSS injection, xss-payloads.com, Pgaijin66, materaj, ismailtasdelen payload lists, rvrsh3ll gist, netsec.expert 2020 XSS article, and Intigriti blind XSS hunting guide.

References section for the XSS document. Cites: hackcommander WAF phishing vector writeup, Holtmann List-Unsubscribe XSS/SSRF post, HackerOne report 2902856 (Nextcloud SSRF), r3verii JS-in-JS credential stealer walkthrough, MDN eval(), ysamm CAPIG XSS postMessage+supply-chain writeup, and MobSF stored XSS advisory GHSA-8hf7-h89p-3pqj.

HackTricks network services pentesting reference for WS-Discovery on UDP port 3702. Documents the SOAP-over-UDP multicast protocol (address 239.255.255.250) used by devices to announce presence via Hello/Bye and respond to Probe/Resolve queries. Nmap wsdd-discover output shows device enumeration including NetworkVideoTransmitter and PrintDeviceType endpoints on local networks.

This chunk introduces rlogin (port 513/tcp) pentesting basics. Rlogin is a legacy remote administration protocol with weak authentication, superseded by SSH. Identifying an open 513/tcp login service signals a high-value target for unauthenticated or trust-based access exploitation.

This chunk covers Rsh (port 514) pentesting fundamentals. Rsh authenticates via .rhosts and /etc/hosts.equiv using IP-based trust, making it vulnerable to IP spoofing attacks on the local network. .rhosts files on NFS-mounted home directories expand the attack surface further.

HackTricks network services pentesting reference for EtherNet/IP on TCP/UDP port 44818. Covers the Rockwell Automation industrial protocol used in ICS/SCADA environments (water plants, manufacturing). Device identification via List Identities message (0x63) sent to TCP/44818; relevant to OT network reconnaissance and industrial control system attack surface mapping.

This chunk is a reference for SMTP protocol commands relevant to SMTP pentesting. Commands VRFY and EXPN enable user enumeration; HELO/EHLO initiate sessions; MAIL FROM/RCPT TO drive spoofed email delivery; AUTH targets credential exposure. All commands are directly usable in manual SMTP interaction for T1566 phishing infrastructure testing.

This chunk details post-auth RCE in Bolt CMS via Twig SSTI. After admin login at /bolt, attacker edits index.twig in the active theme to inject a Twig payload using filter('system') for a reverse shell over /dev/tcp. Cache must be cleared via Maintenance before payload execution triggers on next page load.

Top-level index page for cloud storage bucket pentesting under HackTricks web services coverage. Points to AWS S3 unauthenticated enumeration and abuse techniques, covering bucket discovery, misconfiguration exploitation, and public access testing via the HackTricks Cloud wiki (T1530 Data from Cloud Storage Object).

Overview of Firebase as a mobile Backend-as-a-Service target in web pentesting. Introduces Firebase's SDK-driven architecture as attack surface and references GCP Firebase enumeration techniques for identifying misconfigured Realtime Database and Firestore instances exposed without authentication.

HackTricks network services pentesting reference for Echo service on port 7 TCP/UDP. Documents that the echo service reflects all received data unmodified and can be exploited for denial of service by looping two echo services against each other, generating a packet flood that takes both hosts out of service. Default port 7 open on both TCP and UDP.

Flask HTTP parser inconsistency enabling SSRF via "@"-prefixed request paths. When a Flask proxy app constructs upstream URLs by concatenating SITE_NAME with user-supplied path, a GET @attacker.com request redirects the HTTP client to the attacker-controlled host, bypassing the intended target. Technique documented in HTTP parser inconsistency research.

This section covers JSP getContextPath abuse, a link manipulation and XSS technique where a crafted URL exploits how a JSP application constructs href attributes via getContextPath(), redirecting all page links to an attacker-controlled domain. The technique uses path traversal sequences (..;/) to manipulate the context path and inject a malicious host into dynamically generated links on the page.

This section covers the mod_cgi technique for bypassing PHP disable_functions restrictions on the HackTricks PHP disable_functions bypass page. It presents a complete PHP exploit script that uses Apache mod_cgi, a writable directory, and .htaccess support to register a custom CGI handler (.dizzle extension), write a bash reverse shell script, and execute it via an img tag — achieving OS command execution despite PHP function restrictions.

This section covers bypassing PHP disable_functions restrictions using pcntl_exec (available in PHP >= 4.2.0 and PHP 5). It provides two exploit code examples: one demonstrating direct shell command execution via pcntl_exec with /bin/bash, and a second showing a web-shell pattern that accepts commands via HTTP request parameters. Part of the HackTricks disable_functions bypass reference page.

This section covers a PHP 5.2 disable_functions bypass technique using fopen() with the 'srpath://' stream wrapper and path traversal sequences to access files outside open_basedir restrictions. Part of the HackTricks disable_functions / open_basedir bypass reference page for PHP pentesting.

XS-Leak technique exploiting JavaScript execution side-channels to exfiltrate secret values character-by-character. Uses cross-origin iframes with a dynamic script-src that conditionally calls window.parent.foo() based on whether the guessed flag prefix matches, allowing the parent page to distinguish correct from incorrect candidates via a setInterval polling loop. CTF exploit example from bi0sCTF.

XS-Leak timing attack using performance.now() combined with forcing a heavy server-side task to amplify response-time differences. Embeds the target URL in an <object> element with large dimensions, measures load time via performance.now(), and uses a calibrated threshold (averaged over 3 runs each for found/not-found baselines) to leak flag characters. CTF exploit from justCTF 2022 baby-xsleak challenge.

XS-Leak timing oracle using performance.now() to measure postMessage-based search response time inside a cross-origin iframe. Sends a search payload via postMessage, waits 1ms, then checks if elapsed time exceeds 200ms to determine if the flag prefix matches. Uses Promise.race with a 300ms timeout as a fallback. CTF exploit from NiteCTF 2022 js-api challenge.

XS-Leak technique exploiting Chrome's 2MB URL length limit as a cross-origin oracle. Opens a target search URL padded with a ~2MB fragment; if the URL exceeds the limit the window navigates away and w.origin becomes inaccessible (throws), revealing that the guessed character does NOT appear. Includes a client-side HTML exploit and a Flask server to collect eliminated characters. CTF unintended solution from HackTM CTF 2023 Secrets challenge.

Phone number injection vulnerabilities. Covers appending injection payloads (XSS, SQLi, SSRF) to phone number input fields to exploit back-end parsing and bypass validations. Also covers OTP bypass and brute-force techniques against phone-number-based authentication flows.

Web vulnerability polyglot payload cheatsheet. A single-field scan string covering SSTI ({{7*7}}), command injection (sleep-based), HTTP response splitting / CRLF injection, path traversal (/etc/passwd, Windows hosts), open redirect, SSRF (Burp Collaborator URLs), ReDoS regex patterns, ESI injection, XSS (event handlers, img onerror, javascript: URIs, String.fromCharCode), and XSL/ESI server-side injection probes. Useful for quick multi-vuln fuzzing.

postMessage data theft via iframe race condition — blocking the parent page. Technique from Terjanq CTF writeup: attacker sends a large Uint8Array postMessage to keep the parent page's JS event loop busy, allowing an injected blob-origin iframe to execute a payload and register a listener before the parent sends sensitive data. Covers null-origin blob isolation, async race timing with setTimeout, and cross-origin postMessage interception via XSS in iframes.

postMessage data theft by redirecting a nested child iframe location. When a page missing X-Frame-Options embeds a sub-iframe that receives sensitive postMessage data via wildcard origin (*), an attacker outer frame can overwrite the child iframe's location (frames.location) to an attacker-controlled URL, diverting the postMessage. Includes a Google Docs VRP exploit PoC using setInterval to repeatedly reset the nested iframe src.

HackTricks index entry for ASP.NET __VIEWSTATE deserialization exploitation when the MAC secret is known. References Soroush Secproject's 2019 blog post covering how to craft a malicious ViewState payload to achieve remote code execution on ASP.NET WebForms applications via insecure deserialization of the ViewState parameter.

HackTricks index entry for Java JSF (JavaServer Faces) ViewState deserialization vulnerabilities. Points to resources on misconfigured JSF ViewStates leading to severe RCE, including the Alphabot Security post and a HackTheBox Arkham writeup demonstrating .faces ViewState deserialization exploitation to achieve remote code execution.

HackTricks page covering PHP 5.2.3 disable_functions and safe_mode bypass on Windows using the win32std extension. Demonstrates how win_shell_execute() circumvents the disabled system() function to execute cmd.exe, bypassing both safe_mode=On and disable_functions restrictions. Tested on XP Pro SP2 with Apache and CLI.

HackTricks page covering PHP <= 5.2.9 safe_mode bypass on Windows exploiting the OS-level equivalence of forward and backward slashes in path handling. The PoC (Abysssec advisory) uses exec() with a backslash-escaped path to write and run a cmd.bat batch file, capturing command output in a text file, bypassing safe_mode restrictions.

Cypher injection against Neo4j graph databases. Index card pointing to external research (Varonis neo4jection blog and InfoSecWriteups article) covering how unsanitized user input in Cypher queries can be exploited to exfiltrate graph data, secrets, and cloud credentials — the graph-database analogue of SQL injection.

HackTricks page covering PHP safe_mode bypass using proc_open() combined with a custom LD_PRELOAD environment variable pointing to a malicious shared object (.so). The technique injects a crafted environment into the child process spawned by proc_open to achieve code execution, bypassing safe_mode restrictions on Linux systems.

HackTricks entry covering Ruby _json pollution, a parameter pollution technique in Ruby web frameworks. When non-hashable values (e.g. arrays) are submitted in a request body, Ruby stores them under the _json key. An attacker can inject arbitrary values via _json to bypass authorization checks that validate one parameter but act on _json, enabling auth bypass attacks.

HackTricks page covering PHP 5.2.4 disable_functions and safe_mode bypass using the ionCube Loader extension (v6.5, ioncube_loader_win_5.2.dll). Demonstrates use of ioncube_read_file() to read arbitrary files (boot.ini, system.ini) even when readfile is disabled, enabling sensitive file disclosure via directory traversal on Windows. Also notes ioncube_write_file() as an additional attack surface.

HackTricks page covering PHP 5.x disable_functions bypass via CVE-2014-6271 (Shellshock). Exploits the PHP mail() function to inject a Bash function-format environment variable (PHP_LOL) that triggers the Shellshock vulnerability in /bin/sh (bash), executing arbitrary OS commands. Works when safe_mode limits environment variable prefixes to PHP_ and the system shell is bash.

HackTricks page covering Remote Code Execution (RCE) in Rocket.Chat via the admin Integrations panel. An admin can create an Incoming or Outgoing WebHook and embed a malicious ES6/JavaScript payload using process.mainModule.require and child_process.exec to spawn a reverse shell. Includes step-by-step walkthrough and curl-triggered exploitation.

PostgreSQL data exfiltration technique using lo_import to load server-side files into large objects and dblink_connect to exfiltrate data out-of-band. Covers the FBCTF 2019 hr-admin-module CTF challenge as a worked example of chaining these two built-in PostgreSQL functions for blind/OOB SQL injection data theft.

HackTricks entry on PHP phar:// deserialization attacks. Explains how PHP Archive (.phar) files embed serialized metadata that is automatically deserialized when any PHP file function (file_get_contents, fopen, filesize, md5_file, etc.) processes a phar:// stream wrapper path. Includes a full code example: crafting a malicious phar with a __destruct gadget to execute arbitrary OS commands, embedding JPG magic bytes (\xff\xd8\xff) to bypass file upload restrictions, and triggering RCE via a controlled path parameter.

SQLMap usage guide for exploiting second-order (stored) SQL injection, where the payload is saved in one request and executed in another. Covers --second-url and --second-req flags, and demonstrates writing a custom SQLMap tamper script in Python to handle multi-step flows (register, logout, login, trigger) where simple URL parameters are insufficient.

HackTricks entry on the Cookie Bomb attack. Describes a client-side Denial of Service technique where an attacker plants a large number of oversized cookies on a target domain and its subdomains, causing the victim's browser to send HTTP requests that exceed server size limits and are rejected. Results in a per-user DoS affecting the entire domain scope. References HackerOne report #57356 and the 'Cookie Monster in Your Browsers' presentation.

HackTricks entry on Cookie Jar Overflow, a browser cookie manipulation technique. Browsers enforce a per-domain cookie limit; flooding the jar with ~700 cookies causes the oldest ones to be evicted. Attackers exploit this to delete and overwrite specific cookies — including HttpOnly cookies that are normally inaccessible to JavaScript — by forcing eviction and re-setting the target cookie with an attacker-controlled value. Includes JavaScript PoC and links to a lab.

HTTP Connection Contamination / HTTP connection coalescing attack. Covers how browsers reuse HTTP/2+ connections across subdomains sharing a wildcard TLS certificate, how reverse-proxy first-request routing causes misrouting to wrong back-ends, and how this enables XSS or other injection attacks. Includes a JavaScript fetch-based test snippet and notes on the expanded attack surface in HTTP/3 where IP-address matching is relaxed.

Introductory overview of XS-Search/XS-Leaks on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Defines the core attack model: Vulnerable Web, Attacker's Web, Inclusion Method, Leak Technique, and the two States the attacker distinguishes between when extracting cross-origin information via side-channel vulnerabilities.

Taxonomy of detectable differences used in XS-Leaks attacks on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers the six observable signal categories: HTTP Status Code, Web API Usage, Redirects, Page Content variations, HTTP Response Headers (X-Frame-Options, Content-Disposition, CORP), and Timing disparities.

Overview of inclusion methods for XS-Leaks on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes four cross-origin resource embedding techniques: HTML Elements (stylesheets, images, scripts), Frames (iframe/object/embed), Pop-ups via window.open, and JavaScript Requests via XMLHttpRequest or Fetch API.

Survey of leak technique categories in XS-Leaks on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers Event Handlers (onload/onerror), Error Messages, Global Limits (browser memory/connection caps), Global State (History API entries), Performance API timing, and Readable Cross-Origin Attributes such as window.frames.length.

Section on the XSinator automated XS-Leak testing tool on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes xsinator.com and its companion academic paper, and notes exclusions: service worker leaks, application-specific misconfigurations (CORS, postMessage, XSS), and time-based leaks deemed too noisy.

Introduction to timing-based XS-Leak techniques on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains browser clock sources attackers can abuse — performance.now(), Broadcast Channel API, Message Channel API, requestAnimationFrame, setTimeout, and CSS animations — to create high-resolution implicit clocks for side-channel measurements.

XS-Leak technique using onload/onerror event handlers on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Shows how loading a cross-origin resource via script, object, stylesheet, image, or audio tags triggers onload on success and onerror on failure, leaking HTTP status codes. Includes a script-less nested <object> fallback variant.

XS-Leak technique using onload timing on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes measuring cross-origin resource load duration with performance.now() or PerformanceLongTaskTiming API via HTML element inclusion, leaking page content differences or status codes through network timing.

XS-Leak technique using unload and beforeunload event timing on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains how the time difference between beforeunload and unload events in a framed cross-origin page, measured via SharedArrayBuffer clock, reveals the resource fetch duration.

XS-Leak technique using sandboxed iframe timing and onload on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes applying the sandbox attribute to an iframe to suppress JS execution variance, isolating network timing measurements via performance.now() to detect page load time differences from cross-origin framed pages.

XS-Leak technique using URL fragment hash changes with #ID, error events, and onload on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains how changing only the hash portion of a framed URL re-triggers onload only if the page errored, allowing oracle-style binary extraction of page content without timing.

XS-Leak technique exploiting JavaScript execution via <script> tag inclusion on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes how attacker-controlled JS embedded in a target page runs when the page returns a negative/unexpected response, enabling content-based binary state detection without timing.

XS-Leak technique abusing Cross-Origin Read Blocking (CORB) behavior on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains how CORB stripping response body and headers for CORB-protected Content-Type with nosniff and 2xx status can be detected via onerror, leaking status code and content-type information.

XS-Leak technique using the onblur event and fragment ID focusing on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers loading a cross-origin page in an iframe with a #id_value anchor — if the element with that ID exists, the iframe gains focus and subsequently triggers onblur on the attacker page. Also applicable with <portal> tags.

XS-Leak technique exploiting postMessage broadcasts on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes how cross-origin pages with improperly scoped targetOrigin leak sensitive data through postMessage, and how message presence or absence serves as an authentication oracle to infer user login state.

XS-Leak technique exploiting the browser global WebSocket connection limit on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes exhausting the maximum WebSocket object count from an attacker frame/popup; the number of resulting JavaScript exceptions equals the number of WebSocket connections in use by the target page.

XS-Leak technique using the Payment Request API global limit on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains that only one Payment Request can be active at a time; an attacker periodically attempts to show the Payment API UI and detects a JavaScript exception if the target page is already using it.

XS-Leak technique timing the JavaScript single-threaded event loop on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes dispatching attacker-controlled events and measuring delays caused by cross-origin tasks sharing the same event pool, inferring execution time of other origins' code without direct data access.

XS-Leak technique using a busy/blocked event loop to measure cross-origin execution time on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains intentionally blocking the JS event loop and timing when it becomes available again; notably this method can bypass Site Isolation by observing shared-thread timing impacts.

XS-Leak technique exploiting the global browser socket connection pool on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes saturating 255 of 256 global sockets, timing the target page via the 256th socket, and measuring when a 257th request is queued to infer target page load duration.

XS-Leak technique exploiting Chrome's per-origin 6-connection socket limit on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Extends the global connection pool attack to a single destination: blocking 5 of 6 connections to the same origin and timing the 6th to detect when the victim page issues additional requests to that endpoint.

Overview of the Performance API and Resource Timing API as XS-Leak tools on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers performance.getEntries/getEntriesByName for timing cross-origin resources, the Timing-Allow-Origin header, and how absent Performance API entries can reveal X-Frame-Options framing policy.

XS-Leak technique: Performance API Error Leak on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains that HTTP error responses produce no resource timing entry in the Performance API, enabling status code differentiation (success vs. error) across origins via iframe or HTML element inclusion.

XS-Leak technique: Style Reload Error Leak on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes a Chrome browser bug where failed resource loads result in the resource being fetched twice, producing duplicate Performance API entries detectable by an attacker as an indicator of an error response.

XS-Leak technique: Request Merging Error Leak on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Notes that error-producing requests cannot be merged in Chrome, distinguishable via Performance API; references the XSinator test case for source code details.

XS-Leak technique: Empty Page Leak via Performance API on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains that some browsers do not create a resource timing entry for empty HTTP response bodies, allowing an attacker to detect whether a framed cross-origin page returned empty content.

XS-Leak technique: XSS-Auditor Leak via Performance API on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes how in Safari (SA), pages blocked by the legacy XSS Auditor do not generate Performance API entries, enabling detection of specific page content by injecting crafted payloads that trigger the auditor's filter.

XS-Leak technique: X-Frame-Options detection via Performance API absence on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains that a cross-origin page blocked from iframe rendering by X-Frame-Options (or embed) does not create a performance entry, revealing the presence of the header.

XS-Leak technique: Download Detection via Performance API on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Shows that resources delivered with Content-Disposition: attachment do not create a performance timing entry across all major browsers, allowing attackers to detect file downloads cross-origin.

XS-Leak technique: Redirect Start Leak via Performance API on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes how Safari exposes non-zero redirectStart timing data for cross-origin resources in violation of the spec, allowing an attacker to detect server-side redirects by querying the Performance API.

XS-Leak technique: Duration Redirect Leak via Performance API on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains that in Chrome, redirect responses produce a negative duration value in the performance timing entry, enabling detection of cross-origin redirects via the Fetch API.

XS-Leak technique: CORP (Cross-Origin Resource Policy) Leak via Performance API on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers two signals: in Chrome an empty nextHopProtocol entry indicates the CORP header is set; in Safari no performance entry is created at all for CORP-protected resources.

XS-Leak technique: Service Worker detection via Performance API on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains that resources served from a service worker cache via iframe load faster; the Performance API timing distinguishes cache-served from network-served resources, revealing whether a service worker is registered for the origin.

XS-Leak technique: Cache probing via Performance API on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes using the Performance API to check whether a specific resource is stored in the browser cache by comparing timing entries, including a POST-based cache leak variant.

XS-Leak technique: Network Duration leak via Performance API on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers retrieving the precise network duration of a cross-origin Fetch API request from performance entries to infer page content differences based on response size or server processing time.

XS-Leak technique: Media Error message leak on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes how the MediaError.message property of HTMLMediaElement exposes a distinct string for successfully loaded cross-origin audio/video resources in Firefox, leaking HTTP status code via error message content analysis.

XS-Leak technique: CORS Error message leak on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains that WebKit-based browsers disclose the full redirect target URL inside CORS error messages when a CORS-enabled Fetch request follows a state-dependent redirect, exposing redirect destinations and sensitive query parameters.

XS-Leak technique: SRI (Subresource Integrity) Error leak on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes triggering a deliberate SRI integrity hash mismatch on a cross-origin Fetch request; in Safari the resulting error message exposes the content-length of the response, enabling response size inference.

XS-Leak technique: CSP Violation detection of cross-origin redirects on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers setting the attacker page's CSP to allow only the target origin; a redirect to a different domain triggers a CSP violation report that leaks the redirect occurrence and potentially the redirect destination URL.

XS-Leak technique: HTTP cache probing via error events on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains invalidating a target resource, navigating to a page that conditionally loads it, then re-requesting with a deliberately bad request (e.g., overlong Referer header); absence of an error confirms the resource was cached, indicating the user's authenticated state.

XS-Leak technique: CSP Directive Leak via iframe CSP attribute in Chrome on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes proposing a CSP policy via the iframe attribute; if the embedded page's policy is stricter it shows an error page, allowing detection of specific CSP directives of a cross-origin page.

XS-Leak technique: CORP (Cross-Origin Resource Policy) header detection via Fetch error on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains that a resource protected with CORP throws a JavaScript error when fetched from a disallowed origin, revealing the presence of the CORP header.

XS-Leak technique: CORB nosniff header detection on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers exploiting Cross-Origin Read Blocking behavior to detect the presence of the X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff header on cross-origin responses via HTML element inclusion.

XS-Leak technique: Cache probing via CORS Origin reflection misconfiguration on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes that if Access-Control-Allow-Origin reflects the Origin header, a CORS-mode fetch succeeds from the server but fails from cache (wrong ACAO value), distinguishing cached from live responses.

XS-Leak technique: Fetch Redirect detection via response.type on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains using Fetch API with redirect: 'manual'; a response.type of 'opaqueredirect' indicates the server issued a redirect, leaking cross-origin redirect occurrence in Chrome and Safari.

XS-Leak technique: COOP (Cross-Origin Opener Policy) header detection on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes opening a cross-origin page as a popup and inspecting the contentWindow or opener property; COOP causes opener to be undefined, revealing the header's conditional application.

XS-Leak technique: URL max length server-side leak on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains exploiting server redirect URL length limits by appending user-controlled data so the redirect exceeds the server's max request length, triggering a detectable error. Also covers the cookie bomb variant for same-site contexts.

XS-Leak technique: URL max length client-side leak exploiting Chrome's 2MB URL limit on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes padding a redirect URL past 2MB so Chrome loads about:blank#blocked instead of the destination; detectable because window.origin remains the parent's origin rather than throwing a cross-origin access error.

XS-Leak technique: Max Redirects limit leak on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers pre-consuming 19 of the browser's 20 allowed redirect hops, then loading the target; if the target redirects, the 20th hop triggers an error, confirming the redirect behavior of the cross-origin page.

XS-Leak technique: History Length leak on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes using history.length before and after navigating a frame or popup to the target, detecting JavaScript or HTML-triggered navigations that increment the history count, inferring cross-origin page state.

XS-Leak technique: History Length with same URL oracle on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains that navigating a frame to a guessed URL then immediately to about:blank only increments history.length if the guessed URL matches the current location (no reload occurs for same URL), enabling URL guessing without timing.

XS-Leak technique: Frame Counting via window.length on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers reading the number of iframe elements in a cross-origin popup or frame using window.length to infer user state or page content differences; includes PDF detection in Chrome via embed frame count.

XS-Leak technique: HTML element property leakage on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Overview of reading cross-origin media element attributes (dimensions, duration) to distinguish page states when dynamic media is generated conditionally based on user data or watermarks.

XS-Leak reference: readable cross-origin HTML element properties on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Details leakable attributes: HTMLMediaElement duration/buffered, HTMLVideoElement videoHeight/videoWidth/webkitDecodedFrameCount, getVideoPlaybackQuality() totalVideoFrames, and HTMLImageElement height/width/decode() rejection.

XS-Leak technique: CSS Property leak via getComputedStyle on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes embedding cross-origin CSS stylesheets and using window.getComputedStyle() to read CSS properties that change based on user state, detecting styling differences that correlate with authenticated or personalized content.

XS-Leak technique: CSS :visited history leak on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers inferring browser history by detecting :visited selector styling differences; modern mitigations limit getComputedStyle accuracy, but indirect methods using mix-blend-mode interaction or render timing differences can still reveal visited state.

XS-Leak technique: ContentDocument X-Frame-Options leak in Chrome on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains that Chrome returns an empty (not null) contentDocument for an object element blocked by X-Frame-Options: deny/same-origin, unlike iframes or other browsers, leaking framing policy and potentially user state via inconsistent header application on error pages.

XS-Leak technique: Download Detection via Content-Disposition header on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers three Chromium-based methods: download bar height change monitoring, iframe navigation event absence when Content-Disposition: attachment triggers a download, and window.open navigation monitoring, to infer user access to download-triggering pages.

XS-Leak technique: Partitioned HTTP Cache Bypass timing attack on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains Chrome's cache partitioning key (top-level eTLD+1 + frame eTLD+1) and how same-site subresource requests share a cache key with top-level navigation, enabling cache timing oracles via rapid location change and cancellation or Fetch timing.

XS-Leak technique: Manual Redirect detection via Fetch API on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Briefly covers using Fetch with manual redirect mode to detect whether a cross-origin response is a redirect, leaking redirect occurrence without following it.

XS-Leak technique: Fetch with AbortController for cache probing on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes using fetch combined with setTimeout and AbortController to abort a request before completion; presence or absence of an error reveals whether the resource was cached, and the technique evicts the resource without caching new content.

XS-Leak technique: Script Pollution / prototype overwrite on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers overwriting built-in JavaScript functions before a cross-origin script tag loads; when the script executes and calls those functions, the attacker's overridden version captures the arguments, leaking data from an otherwise unreadable cross-origin script.

XS-Leak technique: Execution timing via Service Workers on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes an attacker-controlled service worker that starts a timer when a target popup window opens and stops it when the window navigates to the service worker's scope, measuring JavaScript execution delay caused by the target page's processing.

XS-Leak technique: Fetch Timing network measurement on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers using performance.now() around Fetch API requests to measure cross-origin response time, inferring page content or status code differences through network timing side channels.

XS-Leak technique: Cross-Window Timing via window.open on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes measuring how long a cross-origin popup window takes to load using performance.now(), leaking page content or status code differences through network timing without same-origin access.

XS-Leak technique: Image Lazy Loading as an injection-based oracle on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains padding injected HTML with junk characters or large canvas elements so a lazy-loaded image only loads when positioned before a secret token, creating a binary load/no-load oracle for content exfiltration.

XS-Leak technique: Scroll-to-text-fragment combined with lazy image loading on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Describes using the #:~:text= URL fragment to scroll a bot to a guessed secret string; if the text matches, the page scrolls and a lazy image below it loads, providing a char-by-char exfiltration oracle.

XS-Leak technique: Time-based lazy image loading oracle on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Covers an alternative when external image callbacks are unavailable: guessing each character multiple times and measuring total request duration — a loaded image produces consistently longer times than a missed guess.

XS-Leak technique: CSS ReDoS timing oracle via jQuery selector on the HackTricks XS-Search page. Explains that when jQuery(location.hash) evaluates a complex CSS selector, early-exit short-circuit behavior causes measurable timing differences when a specific HTML element ID is or is not present, leaking page content through selector evaluation time.

References section of the HackTricks XS-Search/XS-Leaks page. Lists primary external resources: the XSinator academic paper, xsleaks.dev documentation, the xsleaks GitHub repository, the XSinator online tool, and a CTF writeup x-oracle repository.

MITRE ATT&CK T1029: Scheduled Transfer. Covers exfiltration technique where adversaries time data transfers to specific intervals or times of day to blend with normal network traffic. Used alongside T1041 (Exfiltration Over C2 Channel) and T1048 (Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol).

MITRE ATT&CK T1033: System Owner/User Discovery. Covers techniques adversaries use to enumerate current and common users via whoami, w, who, dscl, %USERNAME%, $USER environment variables, and network device CLI commands (show users, show ssh). Used to shape follow-on lateral movement or targeting decisions.

MITRE ATT&CK T1035: Service Execution. Covers execution technique where adversaries run binaries, commands, or scripts via the Windows Service Control Manager by creating a new service or modifying an existing one. Used in conjunction with persistence (T1050 New Service, T1031 Modify Existing Service) and privilege escalation.

MITRE ATT&CK T1036.001: Invalid Code Signature. Covers masquerading technique where adversaries copy metadata and signature fields from a legitimately signed binary onto an unsigned malicious binary. The resulting file fails digital signature validation but may deceive users or security tools. Distinct from valid code signing (T1553.002).

MITRE ATT&CK T1036.006: Space after Filename. Covers macOS masquerading technique where appending a trailing space to a filename (e.g., evil.txt ) causes the OS to execute the file by its true type rather than its extension, allowing Mach-O executables disguised as text files to run when double-clicked by a user.

MITRE ATT&CK T1036.008: Masquerade File Type. Covers technique of altering a malicious payload's magic bytes (file header), extension, icon, or contents to bypass file validation and input sanitization. Includes polyglot files and examples such as naming a PHP backdoor as test.gif. Commonly used during tool transfer (T1105) and malware upload (T1608.001).

Index page for Windows lateral movement techniques in Active Directory / Windows environments. Lists and links to execution methods: PsExec, SmbExec, WmiExec, AtExec/SchtasksExec, WinRM, DCOM Exec, RDPexec, SCMexec, Pass-the-Cookie, Pass-the-PRT, and Pass-the-AzureAD-Certificate (cloud). Entry point for finding the right remote-execution technique.

HackTricks guide on debugging client-side JavaScript using browser DevTools overrides. Covers how to save a local copy of a remote JS file via Chrome/DevTools Sources > Overrides, inject debugger; breakpoints into the local copy, and have the modified script persist across page reloads — a technique for dynamic analysis and XSS research.

AtExec and SchtasksExec lateral movement techniques for Windows. Covers using the legacy AT command and schtasks to schedule remote task execution with known credentials or hashes. Demonstrates Impacket atexec.py for hash-based remote command execution, SharpLateral for task scheduling, and SharpMove with AMSI bypass. Also references silver-ticket abuse via the HOST SPN.

HackTricks stub page on Shadow DOM security and XSS. Points to an external blog post by Ankur Sundara on Shadow DOM attack surface and a DiceCTF 2022 CTF challenge walkthrough demonstrating Shadow DOM exploitation techniques relevant to client-side XSS research.

Windows local privilege escalation via AppendData/AddSubdirectory permission on service registry keys (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\RpcEptMapper and Dnscache). Covers creating a Performance subkey to load a crafted DLL via WMI PerfData queries, achieving SYSTEM execution. Affects Windows 7 / Server 2008 R2. Includes ACE inspection, proof-of-concept DLL with OpenPerfData/CollectPerfData/ClosePerfData, and post-exploitation/EDR evasion notes.

HackTricks section on VBA/Word macro obfuscation using junk code and macro forms. Explains how the GetObject function retrieves data from UserForm controls and how malware authors hide strings or payloads inside nested text boxes within macro forms to hinder static analysis and reverse engineering.

HackTricks overview of document steganography in Office OOXML files (docx, xlsx, pptx). Explains that OOXML is a ZIP+XML container; hidden payloads can reside in word/media/ assets, _rels/ relationship files pointing to external or unusual parts, or custom XML parts — a reference for forensic analysis and stego challenges.

HackTricks stub on Android device forensics for locked devices. Lists three initial unlock approaches: checking whether USB debugging (ADB) is enabled, attempting a smudge attack (fingerprint oil residue on touchscreen to infer PIN pattern), and brute-forcing the PIN/passcode — a starting point for mobile forensic data extraction.

Overview and table of contents for the OWASP Kubernetes Security Cheat Sheet. Lists the major sections covered: host hardening, component security, dashboard usage, and build/deploy/runtime best practices phases.
Introduction to Kubernetes: defines it as a CNCF-hosted container orchestration engine. Explains the cluster model consisting of worker nodes and a control plane that manages pods.

Describes Kubernetes control plane components: kube-apiserver (API front end), etcd (key-value backing store), kube-scheduler (pod placement), kube-controller-manager (controller processes), and cloud-controller-manager (cloud provider integration).

Describes Kubernetes node components running on every worker node: kubelet (container agent), kube-proxy (network proxy implementing Service concept), and the container runtime (software responsible for running containers).

Section 1 overview: securing Kubernetes hosts across bare metal, on-premise, and cloud deployments. Recommends OS patching, hardening, firewall rules, and configuration management to reduce attack vectors on cluster nodes.

Kubernetes version update guidance: always run latest stable release, update source images and redeploy containers rather than patching running containers directly, use Kubernetes rolling updates feature for zero-downtime upgrades.

Kubernetes release schedule policy: project maintains the three most recent minor releases with backported security fixes. Recommends using rolling updates and node pool migrations to upgrade clusters with minimal downtime; references version skew policy.

Section 2 overview: securing Kubernetes components. Lists topics: dashboard security, etcd access restriction, sensitive port network controls, API access control, RBAC implementation, and Kubelet access limits.

Securing the Kubernetes Dashboard: references Tesla cryptocurrency-mining attack via over-privileged dashboard service account. Recommends RBAC, no public exposure, MFA via OIDC id_tokens or Kubernetes Impersonation, and removing cluster-admin bindings left from pre-v1.8 installations.

Restricting access to etcd: explains that write access to etcd equals root on the cluster and read access enables privilege escalation. Direct writes bypass PodSecurityPolicies. Recommends mutual TLS client certificate auth and firewall isolation of etcd from all but the API server.

Limiting access to the primary etcd instance: full keyspace read/write access equals cluster-admin. Recommends separate etcd instances for non-critical components or etcd ACLs restricting access to a subset of the keyspace.

Controlling network access to Kubernetes sensitive ports: lists default TCP ports for control plane (6443 API, 2379-2380 etcd, 10250 Kubelet, 10259 scheduler, 10257 controller-manager, 10255 read-only Kubelet) and worker nodes (10248-10256, 30000-32767 NodePort). Recommends firewall rules restricting these ports.

Controlling access to the Kubernetes API overview: API requests control the platform so limiting and securing them is the primary defense. Covers API authorization flow, external vs built-in authentication options, RBAC, and Kubelet access.

How Kubernetes handles API authorization: authentication required before authorization; permissions denied by default; all parts of a request must be allowed by policy. Kubernetes evaluates all request attributes against all policies before permitting access.

Recommended external API authentication methods for Kubernetes: OpenID Connect (OIDC) for short-lived tokens and centralized groups; managed cloud IAM (GKE, EKS, AKS); Kubernetes Impersonation for on-prem clusters. Recommends MFA for all privileged API access.

Built-in Kubernetes API authentication mechanisms (not recommended for production): Static Token File (cleartext CSV tokens), X509 Client Certs (no revocation support), and Service Account Tokens. Explains why each is unsuitable for production clusters.

Implementing RBAC in Kubernetes: explains role-based access control using rbac.authorization.k8s.io API group, combining verbs (get, create, delete) with resources (pods, services, nodes) at namespace or cluster scope. Shows enabling RBAC via --authorization-mode flag on kube-apiserver with NodeRestriction admission plugin.

Limiting access to Kubelets: Kubelet HTTPS endpoints grant powerful node/container control but default to unauthenticated access. Production clusters must enable Kubelet authentication and authorization.

Section 3 build phase: defining secure container images. Explains container images as immutable layered packages; requires approved and scanned base images; recommends strong governance for image builds and storage in trusted registries.

Using a CI pipeline to control container image vulnerabilities: recommends private registry, vulnerability scanning integrated into build pipeline using tools like Trivy or Grype, and image authorization plugins. Failed security assessments must block image promotion to production.

Minimizing container image features to reduce CVE exposure: recommends distroless or minimal images, removing OS package managers and shells from production images to shrink attack surface and improve scanner signal-to-noise ratio.

Using distroless or scratch/empty container images: distroless images exclude shells and minimize package count to sharply reduce attack surface. Scratch/empty images ideal for statically compiled Go binaries; references GoogleContainerTools/distroless.

Section 4 deploy phase overview: requirements for secure workload deployment. Before deploying, operators must know what is being deployed, where, how it runs (privileged/unprivileged), what it can access (secrets, volumes), and whether it is policy-compliant.

Kubernetes namespace isolation for resource segregation: shows kubectl config set-context command to persistently set a namespace for all subsequent commands, and kubectl config view --minify to validate the active namespace context.

ImagePolicyWebhook admission controller for governing image provenance: prevents unapproved images, rejects pods using unscanned images, images from disallowed base images, or images from insecure registries.

Continuous security vulnerability scanning of running containers: recommends regular production scanning of both first- and third-party containers for newly disclosed CVEs and outdated packages using open source tools Trivy, Grype, and Clair.

Applying pod and container security context: explains securityContext YAML property controlling runAsNonRoot, Linux Capabilities, and readOnlyRootFilesystem to eliminate privilege-dependent attack classes across pods, containers, and volumes.
Security context YAML example: pod definition setting readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and runAsNonRoot: true in the securityContext block, demonstrating minimal-privilege container configuration.

Principle of least privilege for container capabilities and role bindings: containers must be granted only minimum privileges, capabilities, and role bindings required for their intended function to reduce overall security risk.

Pod Security Standards and Pod Security Admission Controller: describes three profiles (Privileged, Baseline, Restricted) for enforcing securityContext requirements. Shows namespace labels for enforce/audit/warn modes. References OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno for granular policy beyond the three built-in profiles.

Pod Security Policies (deprecated in v1.25): lists security policy requirements including no root processes, no privilege escalation, read-only root filesystem, masked /proc, no hostNetwork, dropped Linux capabilities, SELinux options, per-app service accounts, and no unnecessary API credential mounts.

Service mesh as a Kubernetes security layer: introduces service mesh concept as infrastructure layer for secure, reliable inter-service communication, simplifying microservice security and operational challenges.

Advantages of a service mesh: observability via tracing and telemetry, mTLS encryption for inter-service traffic, Istio-based ingress/egress control, operational macro-controls, and RBAC management capabilities to restrict privileged user access.

Service mesh RBAC benefits continuation: restricting privileged users to least-privilege, enforcing deny-all defaults, and ensuring roles and responsibilities documentation are in place as a critical enterprise security concern.

Disadvantages of service meshes: adds architectural complexity with proxies and sidecars, requires expertise in both Istio and Kubernetes, can slow infrastructure performance, and forces adoption of an opinionated platform.

Centralized policy management with Open Policy Agent (OPA), Kyverno, and Kubernetes Validating Admission Policy (GA in 1.30): OPA as a domain-agnostic CNCF policy enforcement tool using JSON input/output, integrable with APIs, SSH, and object stores.

OPA for application authorization: provides pre-built declarative policy language (Rego) for writing access rules like 'Alice can write to this repository'; enables distributed authorization for microservices without developing a custom solution.

OPA for Kubernetes admission control: integrates directly into the API server to enforce policies requiring trusted image sources, prohibiting root execution, mandating storage encryption, and controlling internet access; supports out-of-band policy monitoring and CICD pipeline integration.

OPA for service mesh authorization: using OPA policies within the service mesh to enforce compliance regulations and limit lateral movement between microservices without modifying application source code.

Limiting resource usage with Kubernetes ResourceQuota: defines namespace-scoped CPU, memory, pod count quotas to prevent DoS and noisy-neighbor scenarios. Includes YAML example (compute-resources.yaml) limiting pods to 4, CPU 1-2 cores, memory 1-2Gi, assigned via kubectl create.

Kubernetes NetworkPolicy for pod traffic segmentation: prevents compromised pods from attacking neighbors by default allow-all. Shows JSON NetworkPolicy example restricting backend pods to only accept inbound TCP/80 from frontend pods; references Kubernetes Network SIG work.
