Managing Kubernetes Secrets securely: recommends mounting secrets as read-only volumes rather than environment variables, keeping secrets separate from images, and noting pod-to-pod secret isolation.

Encrypting Kubernetes Secrets at rest: etcd holds all cluster data including secrets. Kubernetes encryption-at-rest feature (introduced v1.7, beta v1.13) encrypts Secret resources in etcd to protect against backup exposure or unauthorized etcd read access.

Alternatives to Kubernetes native Secrets: external secrets managers provide cross-cluster/cross-cloud secrets storage with centralized rotation and access control, offering benefits over native Kubernetes Secret resources.

Finding exposed secrets in container images: recommends Trivy and Gitleaks to scan container filesystems for API tokens, passwords, and keys that may be accessible to anyone with access to the unencrypted image at build time, in a registry, or at runtime.

Section 5 runtime phase overview: gaining visibility into running containerized applications to detect and respond to threats. Key monitoring targets: process activity, inter-service network communications, and external network communications.

Pod Security Admission (replacement for deprecated PodSecurityPolicy): enforces security policies at pod admission. Recommends baseline profile as minimum and restricted profile as target for pod hardening best practices.

Container runtime security using Falco (Sysdig): intercepts low-level syscalls to detect shell execution in containers, sensitive path mounts (/proc), unexpected reads of /etc/shadow, and outbound network connections as indicators of compromise.

Container sandboxing technologies to prevent container breakout and kernel exploits in multi-tenant clusters: Kata Containers (stripped-down VMs), gVisor (Go userspace kernel intercepting ~70% of Linux syscalls with ~20 host syscalls), and Firecracker (user-space microVM with seccomp/cgroup lockdown).

Preventing unwanted kernel module loading in Kubernetes: unprivileged processes can trigger automatic kernel module loading via socket creation, expanding attack surface. Recommends blacklisting modules via /etc/modprobe.d/kubernetes-blacklist.conf (e.g., blacklist sctp).

Blocking kernel module loading with SELinux: using a Linux Security Module to deny module_request permission to containers entirely, preventing kernel module loading under any circumstances while allowing manually pre-loaded modules.

Comparing runtime activity across replicated pods to detect anomalies: replicas should behave identically; significant deviations indicate compromise. Recommends integrating Kubernetes security tools with SIEM, PagerDuty, Slack, and Google Cloud Security Command Center for alerting.

Monitoring container network traffic to identify unexpected communications: compare active traffic against defined NetworkPolicies to detect unauthorized connections and tighten policy to reduce attack surface. References inspektor-gadget and PacketStreamer tools.

Rotating infrastructure credentials frequently: short credential lifetimes limit attacker utility. Recommends automating certificate rotation, short-lived token providers, and revoking bootstrap tokens post-node-setup.
Kubernetes cluster-based logging overview: centralized log collection using Fluentd agents per node forwarding stdout/stderr to Elasticsearch/Stackdriver Logging, viewable via Kibana.

Enabling Kubernetes audit logging: records API actions for post-compromise analysis. Recommends monitoring for authorization failures (Forbidden responses) that may indicate stolen credential abuse. GKE and other managed providers expose audit logs via cloud console with alerting support.

Kubernetes audit log format and structure: audit.k8s.io/v1beta1 Event JSON objects recording kind, level, auditID, stage, requestURI, verb, user, sourceIPs, objectRef, and timestamps for compliance and forensic analysis of kube-apiserver requests.

Defining Kubernetes audit policies: policy rules set audit levels (None, Metadata, Request, RequestResponse) per event type. Passed to kube-apiserver via --audit-policy-file flag; policy file must contain at least one rule.

Container-level logging in Kubernetes: writing to stdout/stderr streams captured by container engine; using kubectl log command; persisting logs via sidecar containers sharing a volume to process and forward application log files.

Node-level logging in Kubernetes: container logs stored in /var/log/containers on host, managed by kubelet log rotation. Docker logging driver configuration not supported via Kubernetes API. Systemd service logs retrieved via journalctl.

Cluster-level logging in Kubernetes: systemd services write to journald; containerized components write to /var/log. Covers cluster component logs alongside events and audit logs to provide full Kubernetes system visibility.

Kubernetes events for monitoring resource state changes: events signal exceeded quotas, pending pods, and status changes. Shows kubectl get events -n and kubectl describe pod commands with example output for namespace and pod-level event inspection.

Section 6 supply chain security: overview of container supply chain attack vectors targeting base images, CI/CD pipelines, registries, Helm charts, and third-party libraries. References high-profile attacks: SolarWinds, Codecov, ua-parser-js as examples of supply chain compromise impact.

Best practices for securing the container supply chain: trusted base images, image scanning (Clair, Trivy, Aqua Security), secure CI/CD access controls, image signing with Notary or Cosign, private registries, continuous vulnerability monitoring, and runtime anomaly detection.

Final thoughts: shifting security left into the container lifecycle build phase. Security as an enabler for DevOps teams to deliver production-ready applications with scale, stability, and security through DevSecOps alignment.

Final thoughts: prefer Kubernetes-native security controls (NetworkPolicy, RBAC, Pod Security Admission) over third-party proxies and shims to enforce security policies without colliding with the orchestrator.

Final thoughts: using Kubernetes deployment context to prioritize vulnerability remediation. Example: a CVSS 7+ vulnerability in a privileged internet-facing container is higher priority than the same CVE in an isolated test environment.

References section: 20 external links to Kubernetes official docs, CNCF blog posts, security guides (StackRox, NeuVector), the Tesla cryptomining incident writeup, OPA documentation, service mesh guides, and logging/observability resources.

HackTricks reference on Burp Suite Intruder payload types: Simple List, Runtime File (large wordlists), Case Modification, Numbers (range/step/random), and Brute Forcer (charset + length). Also mentions Collabfiltrator for out-of-band command output via DNS to Burp Collaborator, and the http-script-generator extension.

MSI Wrapper technique for Windows privilege escalation and payload delivery. Covers using the free exemsi.com tool to wrap a malicious binary or .bat script into an MSI installer package. Useful for bypassing restrictions by delivering payloads as installer files; configuration screenshots highlight key install-elevation settings.

HackTricks stub on hardware fault injection attacks (circuit glitching). Describes introducing external disturbances into electronic circuits to alter execution, leak information, or bypass security restrictions. Covers the general concept of voltage/clock/EM/laser glitching as a hardware hacking technique; detailed methods listed as forthcoming.

Introduction to Industrial Control Systems (ICS) hacking section on HackTricks. Covers the scope of ICS/SCADA/PLC security, explains why these systems are hard to update and commonly vulnerable, and frames the methodology: information gathering and reconnaissance before exploiting legacy protocols and standards developed in the 1990s. Applicable to both offensive pentesting and defensive blue-teaming of industrial environments.

Reference list of OSINT and reconnaissance online platforms with APIs. Covers haveibeenpwned (credential breach lookup), IPQuery.io (IP geolocation and OSINT, non-commercial), DNSDumpster (DNS reconnaissance), Netcraft (site technology fingerprinting), and NMMapper/subdomainfinder (subdomain enumeration). Useful for passive reconnaissance and external attack surface mapping during pentesting engagements.

MITRE ATT&CK T1001.002 — Data Obfuscation: Steganography. Describes adversaries embedding covert C2 traffic inside image or document files using steganographic techniques to evade detection. Sub-technique of T1001 (Data Obfuscation) under the Command and Control tactic.

MITRE ATT&CK T1001 — Data Obfuscation (parent technique). Describes adversary methods for hiding C2 traffic without necessarily encrypting it, including junk data injection, steganography, and legitimate protocol impersonation. Parent of sub-techniques T1001.001–T1001.003. Command and Control tactic. Referenced in Bitdefender FunnyDream campaign analysis.

MITRE ATT&CK T1002 Data Compressed: describes how adversaries compress collected data before exfiltration using tools such as 7zip, RAR, ZIP, or zlib to reduce transfer size and improve portability. The compression step is performed separately from the exfiltration channel.

Overview of the Flipper Zero multi-tool device for hardware and radio hacking. Lists its core capabilities: Sub-GHz radio listen/capture/replay, NFC card read/capture/emulate, 125kHz RFID tag read/capture/emulate, infrared signal capture/send, iButton emulation, BadUSB attacks, and U2F security key use. Links to sub-pages for each capability and the awesome-flipperzero community resource list.

MITRE ATT&CK T1003.002 OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager (SAM): covers extraction of local Windows account password hashes from the SAM database via in-memory techniques (Mimikatz, pwdumpx, gsecdump, secretsdump.py) or Registry export (reg save HKLM\sam). Requires SYSTEM-level access; Creddump7 used for offline hash processing.

Flipper Zero iButton read and emulation guide. Describes the physical contact positioning required to read a real iButton key (blue area placement) and correctly emulate it against an iButton reader (green area contact). Covers the hardware interaction technique for cloning Dallas/Maxim 1-Wire iButton access tokens using the Flipper Zero device.

MITRE ATT&CK T1003.003 OS Credential Dumping: NTDS: covers theft of the Active Directory domain database (NTDS.dit) from domain controllers to extract all AD password hashes. Techniques include Volume Shadow Copy, secretsdump.py, ntdsutil.exe, and Invoke-NinjaCopy; also covers hunting backup copies of NTDS.dit.

MITRE ATT&CK T1010 Application Window Discovery: describes adversary enumeration of open application windows using native OS features, scripting interpreter commands, and Native API calls to identify what software is running, locate data targets, and detect or evade security tooling on the host.

HackTricks overview of web techniques for stealing sensitive information (cookies, credit card data, session secrets) disclosed by a page. Covers four attack vectors: CORS bypass (Ajax requests from a malicious origin), XSS (cross-site scripting to exfiltrate data), Dangling Markup / HTML scriptless injection (stealing data without script tags), and Clickjacking (tricking users into submitting sensitive data). Index page linking to dedicated sub-pages for each technique.

MITRE ATT&CK T1011.001 Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium: Bluetooth: covers adversary use of Bluetooth as an out-of-band exfiltration channel when the primary C2 path is a wired Internet connection. Exploits proximity-based Bluetooth links that are typically less monitored than enterprise network egress points.

MITRE ATT&CK T1011 Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium: describes adversary data exfiltration via alternative physical network channels (WiFi, modem, cellular, Bluetooth, RF) separate from the primary wired C2 channel to bypass enterprise network monitoring and data loss prevention controls.

MITRE ATT&CK T1012 Query Registry: covers adversary discovery via Windows Registry queries to enumerate OS configuration, installed software, and security settings using the Reg utility or other API methods. Results are used to profile the host and shape subsequent attack decisions such as lateral movement or payload selection.

MITRE ATT&CK T1016.001 Internet Connection Discovery: adversaries check for internet connectivity on compromised hosts using Ping, tracert, or HTTP GET requests to verify C2 reachability, identify routes, and detect redirectors or proxy servers before initiating command-and-control communication.

MITRE ATT&CK T1027.012 LNK Icon Smuggling: adversaries abuse the IconEnvironmentDataBlock metadata field in Windows .LNK shortcut files to embed external URLs that download malicious payloads past content filters. Used in phishing campaigns and post-compromise lateral payload delivery via scripting interpreters or LOLBins.

MITRE ATT&CK T1017 Application Deployment Software: adversaries abuse enterprise software deployment systems (e.g., SCCM, PDQ) to push malicious payloads across a network, enabling remote code execution on all connected endpoints and facilitating lateral movement, data collection, or destructive actions such as wiping drives.

MITRE ATT&CK T1020 Automated Exfiltration: adversaries use automated scripts or tools to exfiltrate collected data without manual intervention, typically in combination with Exfiltration Over C2 Channel (T1041) or Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048); associated with Gamaredon group activity.

MITRE ATT&CK T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP): adversaries use valid credentials to log into remote systems via RDP/Remote Desktop Services for lateral movement; may chain with Accessibility Features (T1546/008) or Terminal Services DLL (T1505/005) for persistence; requires credential access techniques to obtain usable accounts.

MITRE ATT&CK T1021.007 Cloud Services lateral movement: adversaries authenticate to cloud control planes (Azure, GCP, Microsoft Graph) using federated domain credentials or application access tokens via web console or CLI commands such as Connect-AZAccount, Connect-MgGraph, and gcloud auth login to access cloud-hosted resources.

MITRE ATT&CK T1022 Data Encrypted (pre-exfiltration): adversaries encrypt stolen data before transferring it out of the network to evade detection, using utilities, programming libraries, or custom algorithms; common archive formats include RAR and zip; used alongside C2 or alternative-protocol exfiltration techniques.

Active Directory persistence technique: Custom Security Support Provider (SSP) installation using Mimikatz mimilib.dll. Covers dropping mimilib.dll into C:\Windows\System32\, querying existing LSA Security Packages via registry, adding mimilib.dll to the Security Packages registry key, and harvesting all cleartext credentials post-reboot from the kiwissp.log file. Relates to MITRE ATT&CK T1547.005 (Security Support Provider).

MITRE ATT&CK T1023 Shortcut Modification persistence: adversaries create or modify Windows shortcuts (LNK) and symbolic links to execute malicious tools at user login or system startup; may masquerade as legitimate programs by mimicking icon and name, or silently replace existing shortcuts to hijack execution flow.

MITRE ATT&CK T1025 Data from Removable Media: adversaries search USB drives, optical discs, and other removable media on compromised hosts to collect sensitive files before exfiltration. Covers use of cmd for interactive collection and linkage to T1119 Automated Collection on removable storage devices.

MITRE ATT&CK T1026 Multiband Communication (deprecated): adversaries split C2 traffic across multiple protocols — one for inbound commands and another for outbound data — to bypass firewall rules and evade data-threshold detection. Technique is retired and superseded by more specific sub-techniques.

Active Directory attack: abusing DSRM (Directory Services Restore Mode) credentials on Domain Controllers. Covers dumping the local Administrator NTLM hash from the DC using Mimikatz lsadump::sam, enabling remote DSRM login by setting the DsrmAdminLogonBehavior registry key to 2, and using Pass-the-Hash (PTH) via sekurlsa::pth to access DC shares (C$) or spawn a remote shell. Relates to MITRE ATT&CK T1003 and credential abuse against DCs.

MITRE ATT&CK T1027.002 Software Packing: adversaries compress or encrypt executables using packers such as UPX and MPRESS, or apply VM-based protection, to change file signatures and evade AV/signature-based detection. Covers in-memory decompression and custom packing schemes that leave no known artifacts.

MITRE ATT&CK T1027.003 Steganography: adversaries conceal data or commands inside images, audio, video, or text files to avoid detection. References Duqu malware hiding encrypted data in images and Invoke-PSImage embedding PowerShell commands in PNG files for covert C2 exfiltration.

MITRE ATT&CK T1027.005 Indicator Removal from Tools: adversaries modify malware to strip detectable indicators after a tool is quarantined or flagged by AV. Covers file-signature evasion by iteratively altering the malicious binary to bypass defenses on current and future targets.

Overpass-the-Hash / Pass-the-Key (PTK) attack against Active Directory Kerberos environments. Covers using an NTLM hash or AES256 key to request a TGT without knowing the plaintext password. Demonstrates Impacket getTGT.py, psexec.py, smbexec.py, wmiexec.py, and Rubeus.exe asktgt with RC4/AES256 options, pass-the-ticket (/ptt), OPSEC considerations, and Windows event 4768 detection.

MITRE ATT&CK T1027.013 Encrypted/Encoded File: adversaries encrypt or encode malicious files using Base64, hardcoded keys, password-protected Office documents, or SFX archives to defeat static signature detection. Covers partial obfuscation of C2 addresses, layered encoding, BOM header abuse, and runtime decode via T1140.

MITRE ATT&CK T1027.016: Junk Code Insertion. Covers obfuscation technique where adversaries insert dead code or NOP (0x90) instructions into malware to hinder static analysis and evade signature-based detections. Distinct from Binary Padding (T1027.001); often combined with compression or software packing.

T1036.012 Browser Fingerprint: sub-technique of Masquerading (T1036) where adversaries spoof browser and system attributes — OS, language, platform, HTTP User-Agent string, resolution, time zone — to blend malicious web traffic with legitimate traffic and evade network defenses and fingerprinting systems.

T1036 Masquerading: defense-evasion technique where adversaries manipulate artifact features — file metadata, file type presentation, task or service names, or renamed system utilities (LOLBAS) — to make malicious objects appear legitimate or benign to users and security tools.

T1037.001 Logon Script (Windows): persistence sub-technique where adversaries add a script path to the HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript registry key so the script executes automatically at Windows logon, enabling persistence on a single system with local or administrator credentials.

T1037.003 Network Logon Script: persistence sub-technique where adversaries assign network logon scripts via Active Directory or Group Policy Objects so the script executes at logon initialization with user privileges, potentially applying to multiple systems across the network.

T1037.005 Startup Items (macOS): persistence sub-technique using the deprecated /Library/StartupItems mechanism on macOS (e.g., Sierra) where adversaries place executable files and StartupParameters.plist in the StartupItems directory to run as elevated root during boot initialization.

T1037 Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: persistence technique (parent) covering scripts auto-executed at boot or logon across operating systems, used by adversaries to maintain persistence, perform administrative functions, or escalate privileges; seen in APT29 and Rocke campaigns.

T1039 Data from Network Shared Drive: collection technique where adversaries search and harvest sensitive files from network shares and shared network drives (NFS, SMB, etc.) on compromised systems prior to exfiltration, often using interactive command shells and cmd.exe.

T1043 Commonly Used Port (deprecated, superseded by T1571 Non-Standard Port): adversaries communicate over standard ports — TCP 80 HTTP, TCP 443 HTTPS, TCP 25 SMTP, UDP 53 DNS, TCP 22 SSH, TCP 3389 RDP, TCP/UDP 135 RPC — to blend with normal traffic and bypass firewalls or network detection systems.

T1045 Software Packing (deprecated): defense-evasion technique where adversaries compress or encrypt executables using packers such as UPX or MPRESS, or custom packers, to alter file signatures and evade signature-based detection; includes virtual machine software protection methods as used by FinFisher.

MITRE ATT&CK T1048.001 — Exfiltration Over Symmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol. Covers adversary use of symmetric encryption algorithms (RC4, AES) to exfiltrate stolen data over non-C2 network protocols such as HTTP or FTP, bypassing detection by adding encryption layers outside normal command-and-control channels.

MITRE ATT&CK T1048.002 — Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol. Covers adversary use of public-key cryptography and asymmetrically encrypted protocols (HTTPS, TLS, SSL) to exfiltrate data over channels separate from the main C2 channel, leveraging built-in protocol encryption mechanisms.

MITRE ATT&CK T1048.003 — Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol. Covers adversary data theft via plaintext protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS) without encryption, relying instead on encoding or compression techniques such as base64 and embedding data in protocol headers to obfuscate exfiltrated content.

MITRE ATT&CK T1051 — Shared Webroot (deprecated). Describes the deprecated lateral movement technique where adversaries upload malicious content to a web server's shared webroot directory via an open network file share, then trigger execution by browsing to it, leveraging web server process permissions for privilege escalation.

MITRE ATT&CK T1052.001 — Exfiltration over USB. Covers adversary exfiltration of data via USB-connected physical devices, particularly relevant in air-gapped network scenarios where a USB device serves as the final exfiltration point or as a hop between disconnected systems.

MITRE ATT&CK T1052 — Exfiltration Over Physical Medium. Covers adversary data exfiltration using physical removable media such as USB drives, external hard drives, mobile phones, or MP3 players, especially in air-gapped environments where network-based exfiltration is not possible.

Introduction to the macOS Auto Start Locations reference page, based on the 'Beyond the good ol' LaunchAgents' blog series. Covers autostart and persistence locations on macOS 13.4, including required permissions for each technique.

Overview of macOS sandbox bypass via autostart locations. Describes persistence techniques exploitable from within a sandbox by writing files and waiting for common user actions, without requiring root permissions.

Enumeration of launchd LaunchAgents and LaunchDaemons persistence locations on macOS: /Library/LaunchAgents, /Library/LaunchDaemons, /System/Library/LaunchAgents, /System/Library/LaunchDaemons, and per-user ~/Library paths, with trigger conditions and root requirements.

Detailed description and exploitation of launchd for macOS persistence. Covers PID 1 role, ASEP plist locations, agent vs daemon distinction, plist structure with RunAtLoad/StartInterval/KeepAlive keys, PreLoginAgents, and launchctl load/unload commands.

Example of a malicious LaunchDaemon persistence chain using password reuse from an infostealer. Shows how a captured sudo password is reused with sudo -S to install a root LaunchDaemon plist at /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.finder.helper.plist and silently start an agent via nohup.

Deep dive into launchd internals: its role as first user-mode process (PID 1), daemon types it spawns (timer, network, path, IOKit, Mach port, UserEventAgent), and notable services like atd, crond, cups-lpd, xscertd, and postfix.master.
Introduction to shell startup files as macOS sandbox bypass and TCC bypass vector. References theevilbit writeups beyond_0001 and beyond_0018 covering zsh and xterm startup file abuse.

Enumeration of shell startup file persistence locations on macOS for zsh (~/.zshrc, ~/.zlogin, ~/.zshenv, ~/.zprofile, /etc/zshenv, etc.), bash (~/.bashrc), and xterm (~/.xinitrc), with triggers and root requirements.

Exploitation of macOS shell startup files (zsh/bash) for persistence. Explains that /bin/zsh is the default macOS shell invoked by Terminal and SSH, and that startup files are automatically sourced on shell initialization.

macOS Re-opened Applications persistence technique via ~/.zshrc execution path. References theevilbit writeup beyond_0021. Sandbox bypass capable but no TCC bypass. Notes the technique did not work reliably in testing.

Exploitation of macOS Re-opened Applications persistence via com.apple.loginwindow plist (TALAppsToRelaunchAtLogin). Shows how to identify the UUID with ioreg, read existing relaunch entries with defaults/plutil, and add a malicious app to the list.

PlistBuddy command to add an application (iTerm2 used as example) to the TALAppsToRelaunchAtLogin list in com.apple.loginwindow ByHost plist, enabling persistence via the Re-opened Applications mechanism.

Terminal Preferences persistence technique on macOS via com.apple.Terminal.plist. Overwriting the CommandString key in the Window Settings plist causes Terminal to execute an arbitrary command on startup, exploitable with the 'open' command.

Persistence via macOS .terminal script files. Opening a .terminal file automatically invokes Terminal.app and executes the embedded CommandString. Inherits Terminal's TCC privileges including Full Disk Access if granted.

Payload construction for macOS .terminal script persistence. Demonstrates crafting a plist-based .terminal file with CommandString set to copy ~/Documents, usable as a data-theft or code-execution primitive when opened by the victim.

Reverse shell delivery via macOS .terminal script file using base64-encoded bash reverse shell payload. Also notes .command and .tool extensions trigger Terminal execution. Warns command is visible in terminal window.
Introduction to macOS Audio Plugins as a sandbox bypass and partial TCC bypass persistence vector. References theevilbit beyond_0013 and SpecterOps Audio Unit Plug-ins writeup.

Filesystem locations for macOS Audio Plugin (HAL and Components) persistence: /Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/HAL, /Library/Audio/Plug-ins/Components, ~/Library/Audio/Plug-ins/Components, /System/Library/Components. Trigger is coreaudiod restart or reboot.

macOS QuickLook plugin persistence technique. A malicious QuickLook plugin placed in a supported location executes code when a user triggers file preview (spacebar in Finder) for a matching file type.

macOS Login/Logout Hooks persistence technique (deprecated). References theevilbit beyond_0022. Sandbox bypass capable but no TCC bypass. Notes neither LoginHook nor LogoutHook worked in testing on recent macOS.

Exploitation of deprecated macOS LoginHook and LogoutHook persistence via com.apple.loginwindow.plist. Shows defaults write commands to register hook scripts, hook file location, and removal commands. Root hook stored in /private/var/root/Library/Preferences/.
macOS cron job persistence as conditional sandbox bypass technique. References theevilbit beyond_0004. Requires crontab binary access or root. No TCC bypass.

macOS cron, at, and periodic job locations (/usr/lib/cron/tabs/, /private/var/at/jobs, /etc/periodic/). Demonstrates programmatic user cronjob creation via crontab command and periodic daily execution.

iTerm2 AutoLaunch persistence technique on macOS. Scripts placed in ~/Library/Application Support/iTerm2/Scripts/AutoLaunch/ (shell or Python) and AutoLaunch.scpt execute when iTerm2 opens. Also covers iTerm2 'Initial Text' preference command execution via com.googlecode.iterm2.plist.
xbar macOS persistence technique. Shell scripts placed in ~/Library/Application Support/xbar/plugins/ are executed when the xbar menu-bar app starts, enabling user-level code execution persistence.
Hammerspoon macOS persistence overview. References theevilbit beyond_0008. Provides sandbox and TCC (Accessibility) bypass. Requires Hammerspoon to be installed on the target system.

Hammerspoon persistence exploitation on macOS via ~/.hammerspoon/init.lua. The Lua script is executed on app startup and can run AppleScript or shell commands, demonstrated by launching iTerm2 as payload.

BetterTouchTool macOS persistence technique. Attacker-controlled shortcuts and actions stored in ~/Library/Application Support/BetterTouchTool/ can execute arbitrary code when the configured key combination is pressed.

macOS Login Items persistence technique. Covers listing, adding, and removing login items via osascript/System Events, storage in com.apple.backgroundtaskmanagementagent, and the SMLoginItemSetEnabled API storing config in /var/db/com.apple.xpc.launchd/loginitems.501.plist.

ZIP file as macOS Login Item persistence technique. A ZIP stored in ~/Library containing LaunchAgents/file.plist is extracted by Archive Utility at login, dropping a LaunchAgent plist that persists across reboots. Can also drop .bash_profile and .zshenv.

macOS 'at' command persistence for one-time scheduled task execution. Explains at tasks are disabled by default, how root enables them via launchctl, usage of 'at now+1', and job inspection with atq and 'at -c JOBNUMBER'.

Detailed inspection of a macOS 'at' job file environment, showing exported shell variables and the job script content. Explains job filename encoding: queue letter, hex job number, and hex epoch-minutes timestamp in /private/var/at/jobs/.

macOS Folder Actions persistence overview. References theevilbit beyond_0024 and SpecterOps writeup. Sandbox bypass via osascript/System Events. Partial TCC bypass with Desktop, Documents, and Downloads access.

macOS Folder Actions persistence exploitation via Automator, Finder context menu, or OSAScript/System Events. Demonstrates JavaScript for Automation (JXA) payload script compiled with osacompile and attached to the Desktop folder using System Events API.

GUI-less setup of macOS Folder Actions persistence. Instructions to copy compiled .scpt to ~/Library/Scripts/Folder Action Scripts, configure via Folder Actions Setup app, and manipulate com.apple.FolderActionsDispatcher.plist for headless deployment.
macOS Dock shortcuts persistence technique overview. References theevilbit beyond_0027. Sandbox bypass capable but requires a pre-installed malicious application. No TCC bypass.

Dock shortcut hijacking technique using a fake app bundle (Google Chrome impersonation). Demonstrates crafting a minimal Info.plist with matching CFBundleIdentifier to replace a legitimate Dock shortcut with a malicious application.
macOS Color Pickers as persistence/sandbox bypass vector. References theevilbit beyond_0017. Requires a specific user action to trigger and lands in a sandboxed environment. No TCC bypass.

Color Picker bundle persistence exploitation on macOS. Compile malicious .colorPicker bundle with constructor attribute, place in ~/Library/ColorPickers. Executed within LegacyExternalColorPickerService XPC sandbox with restricted sbpl entitlements.

macOS Finder Sync Extension persistence technique. Extensions must be signed with Apple developer certificate and sandboxed. Registration via pluginkit -a and pluginkit -e. Example project: D00MFist/InSync on GitHub.
macOS Screen Saver persistence overview. References theevilbit beyond_0016 and SpecterOps 'Saving Your Access' writeup. Partial sandbox bypass (common application sandbox). No TCC bypass.

Filesystem locations for macOS Screen Saver (.saver bundle) persistence: /System/Library/Screen Savers (root), /Library/Screen Savers (root), ~/Library/Screen Savers (user). Trigger is selecting the screen saver in System Preferences.

macOS Screen Saver persistence exploitation. Build .saver bundle in Xcode with Objective-C __attribute__((constructor)) payload, copy to ~/Library/Screen Savers, trigger via System Preferences. Runs inside com.apple.security.app-sandbox via legacyScreenSaver.appex.
macOS Spotlight importer plugins (.mdimporter bundles) as persistence/sandbox bypass vector. References theevilbit beyond_0011. Partial sandbox bypass (application sandbox). Very limited TCC access.

Filesystem locations for macOS Spotlight .mdimporter plugin persistence: ~/Library/Spotlight/, /Library/Spotlight/, /System/Library/Spotlight/, and app bundle Contents/Library/Spotlight/. Triggered when a file with a managed extension is created.

macOS Spotlight plugin (.mdimporter) persistence mechanism. Covers mds/mdworker architecture, dynamic plugin loading without service restart, CFBundleDocumentTypes/LSItemContentTypes configuration, and mdimport -L enumeration command.

macOS custom Spotlight mdimporter creation for code execution. Explains UTTypeConformsTo/UTI handling, precedence of system plugins, and how to build a malicious .mdimporter by modifying GetMetadataForFile in a custom bundle targeting attacker-chosen file extensions.
macOS Preference Pane persistence technique (deprecated/no longer working). References theevilbit beyond_0009. Requires specific user action, partial sandbox bypass, no TCC bypass.

macOS periodic script LaunchDaemons: com.apple.periodic-daily.plist, com.apple.periodic-monthly.plist, com.apple.periodic-weekly.plist in /System/Library/LaunchDaemons. These daemons trigger daily/weekly/monthly script execution.

macOS periodic script persistence via /etc/periodic/ (daily/weekly/monthly) and /etc/defaults/periodic.conf local script overrides (/etc/daily.local, /etc/weekly.local, /etc/monthly.local). Scripts execute as their owner, potentially preventing privilege escalation.
macOS PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) persistence overview. References Linux Hacktricks PAM page and theevilbit beyond_0005. Requires root. Partial sandbox bypass. No TCC bypass.

macOS PAM persistence exploitation by inserting 'auth sufficient pam_permit.so' at the top of /etc/pam.d/sudo. Makes all sudo attempts succeed without authentication. Directory is TCC-protected so a user prompt may appear.

macOS PAM /etc/pam.d/sudo configuration showing pam_permit.so bypass inserted before pam_smartcard.so and pam_opendirectory.so, granting unconditional sudo access. Also demonstrates /etc/pam.d/su configuration for context.
macOS /etc/pam.d/su configuration showing pam_rootok.so, pam_opendirectory.so, pam_group.so (admin/wheel), and pam_launchd.so modules. Context for PAM backdoor techniques on macOS.
macOS Authorization Plugins persistence overview. References theevilbit beyond_0028 and SpecterOps credential theft writeup. Requires root and extra config. Partial sandbox bypass.

macOS Authorization Plugin persistence exploitation. Creates a custom plugin bundle (CustomAuth.bundle) with constructor that appends NOPASSWD sudoers entry, installs to /Library/Security/SecurityAgentPlugins/, registers via 'security authorizationdb write' with evaluate-mechanisms/privileged rule.

macOS man.conf persistence technique via MANPAGER hijacking. Modifying /private/etc/man.conf to point MANPAGER at an attacker-controlled script causes backdoor execution whenever a user runs the man command.
macOS Apache2 (httpd) persistence technique overview. References theevilbit beyond_0023. Requires root and running Apache. Partial sandbox bypass. No TCC bypass (httpd has no entitlements).

macOS Apache2 persistence exploitation via LoadModule directive in /etc/apache2/httpd.conf. Loads a malicious .dylib module with __attribute__((constructor)) payload. Module must be signed with Apple certificate or a custom trusted certificate.

macOS deprecated StartupItems persistence mechanism (no longer used). StartupItem directories in /Library/StartupItems/ or /System/Library/StartupItems/ require an rc shell script and StartupParameters.plist with Provides/OrderPreference keys.

macOS emond (Event Monitor Daemon) persistence technique. An obscure and apparently abandoned Apple logging service whose LaunchDaemon executes scripts from /private/var/db/emondClients, useful as a stealthy persistence method unlikely to be noticed by admins.

macOS kernel extension (KEXT) persistence locations: /System/Library/Extensions (OS built-in) and /Library/Extensions (third-party). Covers kextstat, kextload, and kextunload commands for managing kernel extensions as startup items.

macOS amstoold XPC service hijack technique (historical, no longer present). The com.apple.amstoold.plist LaunchAgent referenced a non-existent binary, allowing an attacker to plant a malicious binary that would execute when the XPC service was called.

GetPID shell helper function used in macOS StartupItem rc scripts. Reads a PID file, validates the process is alive with kill -0, cleans up stale PID files, and returns the PID or exits with status 1.

MITRE ATT&CK T1053 — Scheduled Task/Job. Covers adversary abuse of OS task scheduling utilities across Windows, Linux, and macOS to achieve persistence, privilege escalation, or execution under specific account contexts, including remote task scheduling via RPC and masking execution under trusted system processes.

MITRE ATT&CK T1055.002 — Portable Executable Injection. Covers Windows process injection technique where adversaries copy PE code into a live process's virtual address space using VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread APIs to evade detection, access process resources, and potentially elevate privileges.

MITRE ATT&CK T1055.003 — Thread Execution Hijacking. Covers Windows process injection technique where adversaries suspend an existing process thread, replace its memory with malicious code or a DLL path using OpenThread, SuspendThread, VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, SetThreadContext, and ResumeThread APIs to evade defenses and elevate privileges.

T1055.009 Proc Memory injection sub-technique: adversaries inject malicious code into Linux/Unix processes via the /proc filesystem, using ROP payloads, overwriting /proc/[pid]/maps with dd, and bypassing ASLR to achieve code execution and privilege escalation while evading process-based defenses.

T1056.003 Web Portal Capture sub-technique: adversaries install credential-harvesting code on externally facing portals such as VPN login pages to capture user credentials, used post-compromise to maintain access via External Remote Services and Valid Accounts or as an initial compromise vector.

T1056 Input Capture parent technique: adversaries capture user input to steal credentials or collect information through mechanisms such as Credential API Hooking (T1056.004) or deceptive methods like Web Portal Capture (T1056.003), targeting login pages, portals, and system dialog boxes.

T1059.003 Windows Command Shell sub-technique: adversaries abuse cmd.exe on Windows for execution, leveraging batch files (.bat/.cmd), remote invocation via SSH or Remote Services, and interactive C2 channels; cmd is used to run payloads, scripts, and system control commands with varying permission levels.

T1059.004 Unix Shell sub-technique: adversaries abuse Unix/Linux/macOS/ESXi shell interpreters (sh, bash, zsh, ash, Busybox) for execution via scripts, SSH lateral movement, and C2 channels; shell scripts deliver multi-command payloads and support persistence on Linux, macOS, and embedded/ESXi systems.

T1059.006 Python sub-technique: adversaries abuse Python scripts and interpreter (python.exe) for execution, leveraging built-in packages for file I/O, system interaction, downloading payloads, and executing commands; Python scripts may also be compiled into standalone binaries for distribution.

T1059.008 Network Device CLI sub-technique: adversaries abuse built-in CLIs and scripting interpreters on network devices (routers, switches) to manipulate traffic flows, alter startup configurations, load malicious software, or disable security features; accessible via console, telnet, or SSH.

T1059.009 Cloud API sub-technique: adversaries abuse cloud APIs (AWS, Azure, GCP) via CLIs, Cloud Shells, PowerShell modules, and SDKs to execute malicious actions across compute, storage, IAM, networking, and security services using Application Access Tokens or Web Session Cookies.

T1059.010 AutoHotKey and AutoIT sub-technique: adversaries execute malicious tasks using AutoIT (.au3) and AutoHotkey (.ahk) Windows automation scripts, deploying them as keyloggers, phishing payloads, or modular malware loaders; scripts may be compiled into standalone .exe executables.

T1061 Graphical User Interface (deprecated). Covers adversary use of GUI during operations via remote interactive sessions such as Remote Desktop Protocol (T1076) instead of command-line interpreters, to search for information and execute files. Deprecated in favor of Remote Services T1021.

T1066 Indicator Removal from Tools (deprecated defense evasion technique). Covers adversaries modifying detected malware to remove detection indicators, such as changing file signatures after antivirus quarantine, using Software Packing (T1045) or other obfuscation to evade defensive systems.

T1069.001 Permission Groups Discovery: Local Groups sub-technique. Covers adversaries enumerating local system groups and permission settings on Windows, macOS, and Linux using tools such as Net utility (net localgroup), dscl on macOS, and groups command on Linux, to identify privileged users including local administrators.

T1069.002 Permission Groups Discovery: Domain Groups sub-technique. Covers adversaries enumerating domain-level groups and permissions on Windows, macOS, and Linux using Net utility (net group /domain), dscacheutil on macOS, and ldapsearch on Linux, to identify domain administrators and privileged accounts.

T1069 Permission Groups Discovery parent technique. Covers adversaries discovering group and permission settings to identify available user accounts, group memberships, and elevated privileges. Includes references to tools like BloodHound (CrowdStrike) used to map Active Directory permissions and inform follow-on targeting.

T1070.002 Indicator Removal: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs sub-technique. Covers adversaries clearing system logs on macOS and Linux under /var/log/ to hide intrusion evidence, including auth logs, login records, kernel logs, cron logs, mail server logs, and web server access logs.

T1070.004 Indicator Removal: File Deletion sub-technique. Covers adversaries deleting malware, tools, and artifacts from compromised systems on Windows (del), Linux/macOS (rm, unlink), and ESXi to minimize forensic footprint. References SDelete tool and relation to Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105).

T1070.005 Indicator Removal: Network Share Connection Removal sub-technique. Covers adversaries removing Windows SMB/Admin Share connections using Net utility (net use /delete) to clean up traces of lateral movement and operations involving shared drives.

T1070.010 Indicator Removal: Relocate Malware sub-technique. Covers adversaries copying and moving malware payloads to new locations on victim systems to evade defenses, blend with legitimate files via Match Legitimate Resource Name (T1036.005), target path exclusions (T1564.012), establish persistence, and hinder forensic analysis by separating payloads from earlier execution events.

MITRE ATT&CK T1070 Indicator Removal: describes how adversaries delete or modify artifacts such as logs, downloaded file strings, and command history to remove evidence of intrusion, hinder defenses, impede forensic analysis, and prevent detection across platforms.

MITRE ATT&CK T1071.002 Application Layer Protocol: File Transfer Protocols sub-technique. Adversaries abuse SMB, FTP, FTPS, and TFTP to blend C2 traffic with legitimate file-transfer activity, concealing commands and results within protocol headers or transferred files to evade network filtering.

MITRE ATT&CK T1071.003 Application Layer Protocol: Mail Protocols sub-technique. Adversaries abuse SMTP/S, POP3/S, and IMAP to conduct C2 communications disguised as normal email traffic, concealing commands and results within mail protocol headers or message bodies to evade network filtering.

MITRE ATT&CK T1071.005 Application Layer Protocol: Publish/Subscribe Protocols sub-technique. Adversaries abuse pub/sub protocols including MQTT, XMPP, AMQP, and STOMP via a centralized message broker to conduct C2 communications while blending with legitimate pub/sub traffic to evade detection.

MITRE ATT&CK T1071 Application Layer Protocol: parent technique covering adversary use of OSI application-layer protocols (web browsing, file transfer, email, DNS, pub/sub, SMB, SSH, RDP) to blend C2 traffic with legitimate network traffic and evade detection or network filtering.

MITRE ATT&CK T1073 DLL Side-Loading: Windows technique where adversaries exploit programs with imprecise WinSxS manifest DLL specifications to load a malicious DLL in place of the intended one, masking malicious actions under a legitimate, trusted process.

MITRE ATT&CK T1074.001 Data Staged: Local Data Staging sub-technique. Adversaries aggregate collected data in a local directory or Windows Registry before exfiltration, using cmd or bash to copy files into a staging location, often combined with archive techniques to bundle data.

MITRE ATT&CK T1074.002 Data Staged: Remote Data Staging sub-technique. Adversaries consolidate data from multiple compromised systems onto a single host or cloud instance before exfiltration, reducing C2 connections and evading detection, including staging within cloud VMs created for this purpose.

MITRE ATT&CK T1074 Data Staged: parent technique covering adversary pre-exfiltration staging of collected data in a central location using cmd or bash, including cloud instance staging, to minimize C2 connections and evade detection before exfiltration.

T1075 Pass the Hash (PtH): MITRE ATT&CK lateral movement technique where adversaries authenticate using captured NTLM password hashes instead of cleartext credentials, bypassing standard Windows authentication. Covers hash capture via Credential Access, Windows KB2871997 domain restrictions, and RID 500 administrator hash requirements.

T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts sub-technique in MITRE ATT&CK. Covers adversary abuse of local OS accounts for Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, and Defense Evasion. Includes credential harvesting via OS Credential Dumping (T1003) and lateral movement through password reuse across networked machines.

T1079 Multilayer Encryption: MITRE ATT&CK C2 obfuscation technique references section. Lists external citations including SANS SSL decryption guide, SEI SSL inspection risk analysis, Fidelis DarkComet malware report, and University of Birmingham C2 research paper covering encrypted command and control channel detection.

T1080 Taint Shared Content: MITRE ATT&CK lateral movement technique where adversaries inject malicious code into shared network drives or internal repositories. Covers directory share pivot attacks using LNK Shortcut Modification (T1547/009) and Masquerading (T1036), binary infection via OEP patching, and spread across .EXE, .DLL, .SCR, .BAT, and .VBS file formats.

T1083 File and Directory Discovery: MITRE ATT&CK discovery technique for enumerating files and directories on hosts or network shares. Covers shell utilities dir, tree, ls, find, locate; Native API (T1106) interaction; Network Device CLI (T1059/008) commands such as show flash and nvram; and use of custom tools to guide follow-on adversary actions.

T1085 Rundll32: MITRE ATT&CK defense evasion and execution technique abusing the Windows rundll32.exe process to proxy arbitrary code execution and bypass application whitelisting. Covers Control Panel Item (.cpl) execution via shell32.dll Control_RunDLL, JavaScript execution through mshtml RunHTMLApplication, and Poweliks malware usage.

T1087.002 Account Discovery: Domain Account sub-technique in MITRE ATT&CK. Covers enumeration of Active Directory domain accounts and groups using Net utility commands (net user /domain, net group /domain), macOS dscacheutil, Linux ldapsearch, and PowerShell cmdlets Get-ADUser and Get-ADGroupMember to identify privileged accounts for targeting.

T1090.001 Proxy: Internal Proxy sub-technique in MITRE ATT&CK. Covers adversary use of compromised internal hosts to relay C2 traffic within a victim network, reducing external connections and improving resilience. Tools include HTRAN, ZXProxy, ZXPortMap. SMB peer-to-peer protocol used to blend traffic with normal environment communications.

T1090.002 Proxy: External Proxy sub-technique in MITRE ATT&CK. Covers adversary use of external internet-facing systems (compromised hosts, cloud VPS) as port-redirecting intermediaries to mask C2 server destination. Tools include HTRAN, ZXProxy, ZXPortMap. Victim systems connect to the external proxy which forwards traffic to the true C2 server.

T1090.004 Domain Fronting sub-technique under Proxy (T1090). Covers how adversaries abuse CDN routing by mismatching the TLS SNI field and HTTP Host header to obfuscate C2 traffic destination, including the 'domainless' fronting variant with a blank SNI field.

T1090 Proxy technique under Command and Control. Describes adversary use of connection proxies, port redirectors (HTRAN, ZXProxy, ZXPortMap), and CDN routing to relay C2 traffic, reduce direct infrastructure exposure, chain multiple proxies, and maintain resiliency.

T1092 Communication Through Removable Media technique under Command and Control. Covers C2 between air-gapped or disconnected hosts via physical removable media, requiring both systems to be compromised, with commands relayed from isolated to Internet-connected systems.

T1093 Process Hollowing technique under Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation. Describes creating a process in suspended state, unmapping its legitimate memory, and replacing it with malicious code to mask execution under a legitimate process identity, evading detection.

T1094 Custom Command and Control Protocol technique. Covers adversary use of non-standard or custom-built C2 protocols instead of established application-layer protocols, including mimicry of known protocols and raw socket implementations over TCP/IP.

T1099 Timestomp technique under Defense Evasion. Covers adversary modification of file MAC(b) timestamps (modify, access, create, change) to mimic legitimate files in the same directory, defeating forensic timeline analysis, often combined with filename Masquerading (T1036).

T1100 Web Shell technique under Persistence and Privilege Escalation. Describes placing server-side web scripts (e.g., China Chopper) on accessible web servers to provide remote command execution or shell access, functioning as a backdoor or redundant access mechanism (T1108).

T1101 Security Support Provider technique under Persistence. Covers Windows SSP DLL injection into the LSA process via Registry keys (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages) to gain access to plaintext and encrypted credentials including domain passwords and smart card PINs.

T1102.001 Dead Drop Resolver sub-technique under Web Service (T1102) in Command and Control. Describes embedding obfuscated C2 infrastructure addresses in legitimate public web services (Google, Twitter, social media) to redirect infected victims while hiding backend infrastructure and maintaining operational resiliency.

T1102.002 Bidirectional Communication (sub-technique of T1102 Web Service C2). Describes adversaries using legitimate external web services — social media, Google, Twitter — for two-way command-and-control: sending commands to and receiving output from compromised hosts. SSL/TLS encryption and normal baseline traffic provide cover.

T1102.003 One-Way Communication (sub-technique of T1102 Web Service C2). Describes adversaries using legitimate external web services — social media, Google, Twitter — to push commands to compromised hosts without receiving return output over the same channel. Return traffic may use a separate C2 channel or be omitted entirely.

T1104 Multi-Stage Channels. Describes adversaries building tiered C2 infrastructure where a first-stage RAT collects host info and deploys a second-stage RAT with fuller capabilities (reverse shell). Stages are hosted on separate infrastructure; fallback channels (T1008) guard against first-stage detection and blocking.

T1107 File Deletion (Defense Evasion). Describes adversaries deleting intrusion artifacts — malware, dropped tools, logs — to minimize forensic footprint. Methods include native Windows cmd DEL, Sysinternals SDelete, and third-party secure-deletion utilities. Referenced in the context of APT post-intrusion cleanup.

T1108 Redundant Access (deprecated). Describes maintaining persistence via multiple simultaneous remote access mechanisms — different RATs, valid accounts, external VPNs, web shells — so that removal of one access path does not fully evict the adversary. Superseded by T1136 Create Account, T1505.003 Web Shell, and T1133 External Remote Services.

T1109 Component Firmware (Persistence/Defense Evasion). Describes implanting malicious firmware in non-BIOS hardware components (e.g., drives, NICs, peripherals) so adversary code executes below the OS and survives disk reimages. Related to T1019 System Firmware but targets components with weaker integrity checking.

T1110.002 Password Cracking (sub-technique of T1110 Brute Force). Describes recovering plaintext credentials from stolen password hashes using systematic guessing or pre-computed rainbow tables, typically on adversary-controlled systems offline. Complements Pass-the-Hash (T1550.002) and OS Credential Dumping (T1003); also applies to hashed network-device credentials from T1602.

T1110.004 Credential Stuffing (sub-technique of T1110 Brute Force). Describes using breach-dump credential pairs against target services exploiting password reuse. Lists commonly targeted protocols: SSH, Telnet, FTP, SMB, LDAP, Kerberos, RDP, HTTP, MSSQL, Oracle, MySQL, VNC. Also covers SSO, federated auth, and Office 365 external email services.

T1113 Screen Capture (Collection). Describes adversaries taking desktop screenshots to gather information during post-compromise operations. Can be implemented via remote access tool features or native OS utilities and API calls: CopyFromScreen (.NET), xwd (Linux/X11), screencapture (macOS). Observed in malware targeting Windows and macOS.

T1114.002 Remote Email Collection: adversaries target Exchange Server, Office 365, or Google Workspace to harvest emails using stolen credentials or access tokens. Covers MailSniper tool usage for automated keyword searches against remote email services.

T1118 InstallUtil: Windows .NET command-line utility abused by adversaries to proxy code execution through a trusted Microsoft-signed binary. Covers process whitelisting bypass via RunInstaller attribute on Windows systems using InstallUtil.exe in Framework directories.

T1119 Automated Collection: adversaries use scripting interpreters, remote access tools, or cloud APIs and ETL services to systematically collect internal data matching criteria like file type or location. References File and Directory Discovery (T1083), Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570), and cloud storage enumeration techniques.

T1120 Peripheral Device Discovery: adversaries enumerate attached peripheral devices such as keyboards, printers, cameras, smart card readers, and removable storage on Linux and macOS systems to improve situational awareness and support further attack actions.

T1123 Audio Capture: adversaries leverage OS or application APIs to activate microphones and webcams, or hijack voice and video call services, to record audio from sensitive conversations. Captured audio files are written to disk for later exfiltration.

T1125 Video Capture: adversaries use OS or application APIs to record video or capture images from integrated cameras, webcams, or video call services. Distinct from Screen Capture (T1113); references macOS malware FruitFly and Proton as examples of webcam recording malware.

T1126 Network Share Connection Removal: adversaries remove Windows shared drive and Admin Share connections after use to erase traces of lateral movement. Covers the Net utility command `net use \\system\share /delete` for removing network share connections.

T1132.001 Standard Encoding: adversaries encode C2 traffic using standard schemes such as ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, or MIME to evade detection. Standard encoding may also produce data compression as a side effect (e.g., gzip).

T1132.002 Non-Standard Encoding: adversaries encode C2 traffic using custom or modified encoding schemes that deviate from standard protocol specifications, such as a modified Base64 for HTTP request bodies, to complicate detection of command and control communications.

T1132 Data Encoding: MITRE ATT&CK technique describing how adversaries encode C2 traffic using ASCII, Unicode, Base64, MIME, or other binary-to-text encoding systems to evade detection. Covers command and control obfuscation, data compression (gzip), and encoding schemes that blend with legitimate protocol specifications.

T1135 Network Share Discovery: MITRE ATT&CK technique covering adversary enumeration of shared folders and drives on remote systems via SMB protocol on Windows. Describes use of Net tool commands (net view, net share) for Windows network share enumeration and the macOS sharing -l command. Relevant to pre-Collection reconnaissance and Lateral Movement planning.

T1136.002 Create Account: Domain Account sub-technique. Covers adversary creation of Active Directory domain accounts (user, administrator, service) using net user /add /domain to establish persistent secondary credentialed access across domain-joined systems without deploying remote access tools.

T1136 Create Account: MITRE ATT&CK persistence technique covering adversary creation of local, domain, or cloud tenant accounts to maintain access. Describes how created accounts establish secondary credentialed access without persistent remote access tools, including cloud-scoped service accounts to reduce detection.

T1139 Bash History: MITRE ATT&CK credential access technique for Linux and macOS. Describes how adversaries search ~/.bash_history to harvest cleartext usernames and passwords typed as command-line parameters. Covers the bash history utility, HISTFILE location, and the 500-command default retention limit.

T1142 Keychain: MITRE ATT&CK credential access technique targeting macOS Keychain. Covers adversary access to ~/Library/Keychains storing WiFi passwords, website credentials, certificates, and Kerberos tickets. Describes the security CLI utility and how obtaining login keychain credentials exposes all stored secrets.

T1146 Clear Command History: MITRE ATT&CK defense evasion technique on macOS and Linux. Covers adversary methods to erase ~/.bash_history and suppress shell history logging using unset HISTFILE, export HISTFILESIZE=0, history -c, and rm ~/.bash_history. Also notes history files as a source of harvested cleartext passwords.

T1147 Hidden Users: MITRE ATT&CK persistence technique on macOS. Describes how adversaries create user accounts with userIDs at or below 500 and enable the Hide500Users property in com.apple.loginwindow to conceal accounts from the login screen. Uses dscl to assign low UniqueID values, combined with T1136 Create Account.

T1148 HISTCONTROL: MITRE ATT&CK defense evasion technique on Linux and macOS. Covers adversary manipulation of the HISTCONTROL environment variable (ignorespace, ignoredups, ignoreboth) to prevent terminal commands from being saved to ~/.bash_history, enabling stealthy operation by prepending a space to all commands.

MITRE ATT&CK T1149 LC_MAIN Hijacking (deprecated): describes how adversaries can hijack the LC_MAIN entry point header in macOS Mach-O binaries (introduced in OS X 10.8) to redirect initial execution to malicious code before returning to the legitimate entry point, bypassing application whitelisting on macOS/OS X platforms.

MITRE ATT&CK T1150 Plist Modification: covers adversary abuse of macOS and OS X property list (plist) XML configuration files located in /Library/Preferences and ~/Library/Preferences to redirect code execution, run code in another user's context, bypass application whitelisting, or establish persistence. Involves malware such as the Sofacy Komplex Trojan.

MITRE ATT&CK T1151 Space after Filename: describes a macOS/OS X masquerading technique where a trailing space appended to a filename (e.g., evil.txt with space) causes the OS to execute a Mach-O binary regardless of extension, tricking users who double-click apparent benign files into running malicious executables.

MITRE ATT&CK T1152 Launchctl: describes how adversaries abuse the macOS launchctl utility to control the launchd process, load/reload launch agents and daemons for persistence, execute arbitrary commands, and bypass application whitelisting on macOS. Referenced in context of Sofacy Komplex Trojan malware.

MITRE ATT&CK T1153 Source (deprecated): covers adversary abuse of the Unix/Linux shell built-in source command (or dot operator) to execute scripts and load functions within the current shell context without requiring the file to be marked executable, enabling code execution on Linux and macOS systems.

MITRE ATT&CK T1154 Trap: describes adversary use of the Unix/Linux shell trap command to register malicious command lists that execute upon receipt of specific interrupt signals (e.g., ctrl+c, ctrl+d), enabling code execution or persistence on Linux and macOS systems when shell interrupts are triggered.

MITRE ATT&CK T1155 AppleScript: covers adversary use of macOS AppleScript and the osascript tool to send AppleEvent IPC messages for local and remote interaction with applications, enabling lateral movement via SSH, fake dialog box presentation, keylogging, and launching reverse shells on macOS and OS X platforms.

MITRE ATT&CK T1156 Malicious Shell Modification (also known as .bash_profile and .bashrc): describes persistence via injecting malicious commands into shell initialization scripts (/etc/profile, ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bashrc, ~/.bash_logout on Linux; /etc/zshenv, ~/.zshrc on macOS). References malware families Rocke, Tsunami, Linux Rabbit, Cannon, Pearl_shellbot, and Kaiji.

MITRE ATT&CK T1161 LC_LOAD_DYLIB Addition: describes how adversaries inject malicious dynamic library (dylib) load commands into the LC_LOAD_DYLIB header of macOS/OS X Mach-O binaries to achieve persistence or code execution at load time, and how removing LC_CODE_SIGNATURE bypasses digital signature verification checks.

T1560.002 Archive via Library: adversaries compress or encrypt collected data before exfiltration using third-party libraries such as Python rarfile, libzip, and zlib. Covers preinstalled system libraries including bzip2 on macOS/Linux and zip on Windows, distinguishing library linking from utility execution.

T1560.003 Archive via Custom Method: adversaries compress or encrypt collected data before exfiltration using custom-built methods such as XOR or stream ciphers with no external library dependencies. Covers custom implementations of known compression algorithms to avoid detection through standard tool signatures.

T1560 Archive Collected Data: parent technique covering adversary compression and/or encryption of collected data prior to exfiltration to obfuscate content and minimize network traffic. Encompasses subtechniques using utilities, third-party libraries, or custom methods for archival operations before data transfer.

T1562.007 Disable or Modify Cloud Firewall: adversaries disable or modify cloud environment firewalls including AWS security groups to bypass access controls. Covers creation of permissive ingress rules, removal of network limitations for cryptomining, and enabling C2 communications, lateral movement, or data exfiltration in cloud-hosted infrastructure.

T1562.011 Spoof Security Alerting: adversaries spoof security tool alerts and status indicators to impair defender awareness after disabling legitimate defenses. Covers fake Windows Security GUI and tray icon showing healthy system status post-infection, associated with BlackBasta ransomware, to delay incident response.

MITRE ATT&CK T1562 Impair Defenses: parent technique covering adversary actions that disable or hinder defensive mechanisms including firewalls, antivirus, detection capabilities, event aggregation, update processes, and system shutdown controls. Defense Evasion tactic. Referenced by UNC3886 and Emotet campaigns.

MITRE ATT&CK T1564.012 Hide Artifacts: File/Path Exclusions sub-technique. Adversaries drop payloads into folders or filenames excluded from antivirus scanning to evade detection, exploiting hardcoded AV exclusion paths without needing to modify tool settings (T1562.001). Defense Evasion tactic on Windows, macOS, Linux.

MITRE ATT&CK T1564.013 Hide Artifacts: Bind Mounts sub-technique. Adversaries use Linux bind mounts to overlay a malicious process's /proc directory with a benign process directory, hiding process metadata and executables from ps, top, and other system utilities. Exploited by Commando Cat and CoinMiner campaigns. Defense Evasion tactic on Linux/containers.

MITRE ATT&CK T1564.014 Hide Artifacts: Extended Attributes sub-technique. Adversaries abuse xattrs on macOS and Linux to embed hidden payloads in file metadata, invisible to ls, Finder, and cat. Uses xattr/setfattr commands; payload extracted with xattr -p or getfattr. Bypasses hash-based integrity checks. Defense Evasion tactic, referenced in GroupIB research 2024.

MITRE ATT&CK T1565.001 Data Manipulation: Stored Data Manipulation sub-technique. Adversaries insert, delete, or alter data at rest (Office files, databases, emails, custom formats) to affect business processes, decisions, or hide activity. Associated with APT38 and Lazarus Group. Impact tactic targeting data integrity.

MITRE ATT&CK T1565.002 Data Manipulation: Transmitted Data Manipulation sub-technique. Adversaries intercept and alter data in transit over network connections or between system processes to manipulate external outcomes or hide activity. Associated with APT38 and Lazarus Group. Impact tactic targeting data integrity during transmission.

MITRE ATT&CK T1565.003 Data Manipulation: Runtime Data Manipulation sub-technique. Adversaries modify application binaries or use file association changes and masquerading (T1546.001, T1036) to alter data displayed to end users at runtime, affecting business processes or decisions. Associated with APT38 and Lazarus Group. Impact tactic.

MITRE ATT&CK T1566.003 Phishing: Spearphishing via Service sub-technique. Adversaries send targeted phishing messages through third-party services such as social media, personal webmail, and messaging platforms rather than enterprise email, bypassing corporate email controls. Referenced in Dark Caracal campaign (Lookout 2018). Initial Access tactic.

MITRE ATT&CK T1567.001 Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Code Repository sub-technique. Adversaries exfiltrate stolen data to code repositories such as GitHub via HTTPS APIs, blending with legitimate network traffic. Exfiltration tactic providing cover through commonly allowed services.

MITRE ATT&CK T1567.002 Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage sub-technique. Adversaries exfiltrate data to cloud storage services such as Dropbox or Google Docs over the Internet, blending with legitimate traffic to those services. Exfiltration tactic providing network-level cover.

MITRE ATT&CK T1567.003 Exfiltration to Text Storage Sites: adversaries exfiltrate collected data to public text-sharing platforms such as pastebin[.]com instead of primary C2 channels. Sub-technique of T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service. Distinct from T1567/001 Exfiltration to Code Repository. Covers use of paid and encrypted paste features to conceal exfiltrated data.

MITRE ATT&CK T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service: adversaries abuse legitimate external web services as exfiltration channels instead of primary C2, leveraging existing firewall allowances and SSL/TLS encryption for concealment. Parent technique covering sub-techniques including exfiltration to code repositories and text storage sites.

Introduction to the OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet. Covers the problem of hardcoded credentials, API keys, database credentials, SSH keys, and certificates in source code and config files. Motivates centralized secrets storage, provisioning, auditing, rotation, and access control to prevent leakage.

High-availability requirements for secrets management solutions. Covers reliability for user credentials (SSH keys, root passwords) and application secrets (database credentials, API keys) under incident response conditions. Addresses service volume and startup latency concerns.

Centralization and standardization of secrets management. Covers managing multiple solutions (cloud-native, third-party, password managers), consistent lifecycle management, authentication, authorization, accounting, and avoiding vendor lock-in through documentation and multi-solution governance.

Access control for secrets management systems. Covers applying least-privilege principle to engineers accessing secrets vaults, fine-grained per-object and per-component access policies, and reducing exposure through restricted read/write permissions.

Automated secrets management techniques. Covers secrets pipelines, dynamic secrets generation per session to reduce credential reuse surface, and automated rotation strategies including gradual rotation, write/read key splitting, rapid rotation, and scheduled rotation for static secrets like encryption keys.

Kubernetes sidecar container pattern for automated secret rotation. Covers HashiCorp Vault Agent and CyberArk Conjur Secrets Provider as sidecars authenticating via Kubernetes Service Account, writing secrets to a shared in-memory emptyDir volume, and periodically refreshing short-lived credentials for the main application container.

AWS Lambda serverless function pattern for automated database credential rotation via AWS Secrets Manager. Covers the four-step rotation lifecycle (createSecret, setSecret, testSecret, finishSecret), AWSPENDING/AWSCURRENT version stages, and boto3 put_secret_value and update_version_stage API calls.

Handling secrets in process memory. Covers threat modeling for memory-based attacks, Rowhammer, Meltdown and Spectre side-channel vulnerabilities, process isolation requirements in cloud deployments, memory dump extraction risks, and language-level differences between C/C++ and garbage-collected runtimes for secure memory handling.

In-memory secret protection techniques for .NET and Java. Covers using mutable byte arrays or char arrays instead of immutable String objects, zeroing memory after use, and hardware or OS-level memory encryption to minimize the plaintext window. References OWASP MASTG MASVS-STORAGE testing guidance.

Auditing requirements for secrets management systems. Covers logging secret requests, approvals/rejections, usage events, expiration, reuse of expired secrets, auth/authz errors, updates, and administrative actions. Addresses timestamp integrity, NTP synchronization, and clock-skew monitoring.

Secret lifecycle creation phase. Covers cryptographic strength requirements, minimum-privilege assignment, secure credential transmission via mutually authenticated channels or side-channels (push notification, SMS, email), and multi-factor authentication channel trade-offs. References OpenCRE secret creation guidance.

Secret rotation policy. Covers regular rotation to limit exposure window of stolen credentials, secret lifetime ranges (minutes for perfect forward secrecy to years for hardware secrets), and NIST SP 800-63 guidance excluding routine rotation of user-managed credentials.

Secret expiration policy. Covers time-bounded secret validity, active expiration by consuming systems, expiration-triggered rotation workflows in secrets management solutions, and application-side validation of secret status before use.

Secrets management downtime, break-glass procedures, and backup/restore. Covers maintenance window planning, automated backup frequency, restore testing, encrypted backup storage with restricted access, and emergency break-glass credentials stored in a secondary secrets management system.

Organization-wide secrets management policies. Covers enforcing minimum password complexity requirements, approved encryption algorithms, and best-practice compliance through a centralized secrets management solution and a formal policy framework.

Secret metadata management to prevent vendor lock-in. Covers required metadata fields: creation/consumption/archival/rotation/deletion timestamps and actors, intended consumers, secret type (AES key, HMAC key, RSA private key), manual rotation schedule, and contact information.

Passwordless authentication and OIDC token security. Covers OpenID Connect to reduce phishing and credential stuffing risks, centralized IdP MFA enforcement, short-lived bearer tokens (access/ID/refresh), TLS transmission, HTTP-only cookie storage, token signature and audience validation, and refresh token rotation.

Overview of secrets management in CI/CD pipelines. Covers the role of CI/CD tools in storing and provisioning secrets for build, test, and deployment processes and their interaction with dedicated secrets management systems.

Hardening CI/CD pipelines against secret compromise. Covers treating CI/CD infrastructure as production, security event monitoring, least-privilege developer access, preventing pipeline output from leaking secrets, blocking exec access to runners, and security-reviewed pipeline creation via MR/PR processes.

Secret storage placement options for CI/CD: native CI/CD tooling (GitLab, GitHub, Jenkins secrets) versus external secrets management systems (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Google Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Conjur, Keeper). Covers Encryption as a Service for git-stored encrypted secrets and service-side retrieval patterns.

Best practices for secrets stored in CI/CD tooling (GitHub secrets, GitLab repository secrets, Azure DevOps ENV Vars, Kubernetes Secrets). Covers blast-radius minimization, user access auditing, administrative access reduction, logging and alerting for extraction attempts (Base64 encoding, OpenSSL), rotation, fork isolation, and documentation.

Best practices for CI/CD pipelines using dedicated secrets management systems (AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault, Keeper, Conjur). Covers credential temporality/rotation, scoped authorization, caller attribution, logging, fork safety, and cold-storage backup for encryption keys.

Pattern where secrets bypass CI/CD entirely: consuming services retrieve secrets directly from a secrets manager via Kubernetes service accounts at runtime. CI/CD only holds orchestration-platform credentials, not the secrets themselves, reducing exposure surface.

Authentication and authorization of CI/CD service accounts. Covers designated service accounts scoped to required secrets, attributing pipeline runs to individual users or job creators via certificate identity or token principals, and periodic verification for security alerting.

Logging and accounting for secrets in CI/CD pipelines. Covers attacker exfiltration via double Base64 encoding and OpenSSL in jobs, security alerting on non-standard pipeline manipulation, 90-day queryable log retention, and extended cold-storage archival for forensic investigation.

Dynamic secrets versus secret rotation in CI/CD. Covers triggering rotation in external systems via CI/CD tooling, consumer-lifetime dynamic secrets that auto-invalidate on container termination, and IP-based anomaly detection for compromised dynamic secrets.

Pipeline-generated secrets and git-stored encrypted secrets. Covers sidecar-based decryption pattern, per-environment encryption with separate keys (DTAP), preventing cross-environment secret leakage, and best practices for secure randomness and length in pipeline-generated credentials.

Cloud provider secrets management service selection. Covers using designated cloud-native secret management services versus self-hosted solutions (HashiCorp Vault, Conjur) on cloud compute, and preferring provider-managed rotation to reduce misconfiguration risk.

AWS secrets management: AWS Secrets Manager versus Systems Manager Parameter Store. Covers secret-level IAM permissions, default encryption in Secrets Manager, and Parameter Store limitations including manual encryption, limited auto-rotation, no cross-account access, no cross-region replication, and fewer Security Hub controls.

AWS Nitro Enclaves for high-assurance secret handling. Covers isolated compute environments with restricted operator access, cryptographic attestation to verify enclave identity before provisioning secrets, and trusted execution environment guarantees.

AWS CloudHSM for bring-your-own-key (BYOK) secret storage. Covers hardware security module control over key creation, lifecycle, and durability, automatic scaling and backup, and the guarantee that Amazon cannot access key material stored in CloudHSM.

GCP Confidential Computing for in-use data encryption. Covers Confidential VMs and Confidential GKE Nodes using AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) to encrypt memory during processing, preventing cloud-provider personnel from accessing VM memory contents holding secrets.

Azure Key Vault for secrets management. Covers vault-level permission granularity (vs. per-secret granularity in AWS/GCP), requirement to separate Key Vaults by workload and sensitivity level, and links to Azure Key Vault best practices documentation.

Azure Confidential Computing trusted execution environments. Covers Azure Confidential Virtual Machines and Confidential Containers on ACI using Intel SGX and AMD SEV-SNP for secure enclaves that encrypt data at rest, in transit, and in use against administrators and co-tenants.

Azure Dedicated HSM for enhanced cryptographic control. Covers hardware security module-based key storage with full administrative and cryptographic control and the guarantee that Microsoft cannot access key material stored in Azure Dedicated HSM.

Multi-cloud and cloud-agnostic secrets management solutions. Covers avoiding vendor lock-in through tools like CyberArk Conjur, HashiCorp Vault, and Pulumi ESC that operate across multiple cloud providers and on-premises environments simultaneously.

Envelope and client-side versus server-side encryption of secrets. Covers server-side encryption at rest (cloud-managed), client-side end-to-end encryption from producer to consumer, and PGP-based and scalable cryptographic mechanisms for maintaining confidentiality through transit.

Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) versus cloud-provider-managed encryption keys. Covers data key hierarchy (CMK encrypts data key, data key encrypts secret), key import into AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, and GCP KMS, cloud HSM-backed key generation, and complexity trade-offs of self-managed key material.

IAM hardening for cloud secrets management.
