Index page for web attack surface enumeration focusing on subdomain discovery: querying subdomain databases, brute-forcing DNS names, leveraging Certificate Transparency logs, bulk DNS resolution, technology fingerprinting, and exploiting subdomain takeover vulnerabilities on dangling DNS entries.

Index page for Windows AMSI (Antimalware Scan Interface) bypass techniques including listing AMSI providers, patching amsi.dll AmsiScanBuffer in memory (rasta-mouse method, Adam Chester patch), forcing AMSI errors, disabling PowerShell script block logging, Matt Graeber reflection methods, DLL hijacking (Cornelis de Plaa), PowerShell v2 downgrade, Nishang all-in-one bypass, and amsi.fail online generator.

Index page for Windows DPAPI (Data Protection API) credential theft techniques covering listing credential and master-key files, DPAPI LocalMachine context decryption, Mimikatz DPAPI credential manager extraction, Hekatomb domain-wide credential theft tool, and DonPAPI remote DPAPI credential dumping over SMB.

Index page for Windows security defenses relevant to red-team evasion, covering AppLocker application whitelisting, UAC (User Account Control), DPAPI, PowerShell AMSI, JEA (Just Enough Administration), Constrained Language Mode, Script Block Logging, Protected Process Light (PPL), Credential Guard, ETW (Event Tracing for Windows), Windows Defender AV, WDAC (Windows Defender Application Control), Windows Firewall, and Windows Information Protection.

context: Index page for Windows living-off-the-land download-and-execute techniques covering LOLBins used to fetch and run payloads: PowerShell IEX/DownloadString, cmd.exe, Cscript/Wscript, Mshta, Rundll32, Regasm/Regsvc, Regsvr32 (squiblydoo), Odbcconf, MSBuild inline tasks, Certutil base64 decode, and Bitsadmin file transfer.

Mimikatz Windows credential extraction tool cheatsheet index covering execute commands, extract passwords, LSA Protection workaround, mini dump, Pass The Hash, Golden Ticket, Skeleton Key, RDP session takeover, RDP passwords, Credential Manager, DPAPI, Chrome cookies, scheduled task credentials, Vault, and PowerShell version.

Browser-powered HTTP request smuggling (client-side desync): abusing the victim's browser to send mis-framed requests over shared HTTP/1.1 or H2 connections, causing downstream servers to parse subsequent requests out-of-sync. Covers key constraints (no custom headers), target primitives (path confusion, query injection, form POST body shaping), and impacts including cache poisoning and front-end header leakage.

Browser HTTP request smuggling references section: links to PortSwigger research on browser-powered desync attacks, PortSwigger Academy client-side desync labs, and guidance on distinguishing genuine HTTP request smuggling from HTTP pipelining false positives.

Web login bypass techniques overview: checking page comments, direct restricted page access, missing parameter attacks, PHP array comparison errors (user[]=a), JSON content-type bypass with bool true, Node.js mysqljs password[password]=1 SQL injection quirk, and credential brute-forcing with Cewl wordlists and default credential lists.

XPath injection authentication bypass payloads for login forms: a collection of XPath boolean injection strings (e.g., ' or '1'='1, ' or true() or ', contains() predicates, position()=2) used to circumvent authentication logic in XML/XPath-backed login endpoints.

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) vulnerability class in ASP.NET covering Razor, ASPX, and other templating engines where unsanitized user input is embedded into server-side templates, enabling arbitrary code execution on the server.

MySQL LOAD_FILE() SSRF via SQL injection: using the LOAD_FILE() function with secure_file_priv disabled to initiate out-of-band network requests. On Windows, UNC path support enables NTLMv2 hash exfiltration over TCP port 445 via SMB, limited to that port without modification.

MySQL RCE via User Defined Functions (UDF): loading external libraries (e.g., lib_mysqludf_sys) into MySQL's plugin_dir using hex/base64-encoded payloads to enable OS command execution or HTTP SSRF. Requires file_priv=Y, secure_file_priv disabled, and writable @@plugin_dir. SQLMap supports UDF injection automation; blind injection uses DNS smuggling.

Curated directory of notable security researcher and bug bounty hunter Twitter/X accounts including researchers from HackerOne, Bugcrowd, Intigriti, and Synack, covering web security, RCE research, iOS security, and pentesting tool authors such as Mimikatz creator GentilKiwi and PayloadsAllTheThings author pentest_swissky.

XS-Search connection pool timing attack exploit (Sekai CTF safelist challenge): attacker injects img tags loading /js/purify.js to saturate Chrome's 6-connection-per-origin limit, then times a request to detect whether the target note contains the flag prefix or the injected payload, leaking content character by character via network timing side-channel.

XS-Search connection pool exploit JavaScript implementation: full CTF exploit script using checkLetter() function that injects img tags, removes competing notes, measures purify.js load time via onerror timing, and exfiltrates flag characters using navigator.sendBeacon when timing threshold exceeds 100ms, iterating the alphabet to reconstruct the flag.

Chrome cache to XSS technique: exploiting interaction between Chrome's back/forward cache (bfcache, stores full JS heap) and disk cache (stores fetched resources) to render a cached JSON or error API response as HTML in the browser, enabling XSS by triggering history.back() after a fetch caches a target API endpoint.

Chrome cache to XSS reproduction steps: open target API URL causing 500 error, navigate to the app root to cache the API response as disk cache, use history.back() to render the cached JSON response as a page in the browser, verified via Chrome DevTools network panel showing disk cache hit.

Containerd ctr privilege escalation (PE 1): abusing the ctr CLI when available on a host to list container images and launch a container with the host root filesystem bind-mounted (src=/, dst=/), gaining read-write access to the host from inside the container as a privilege escalation vector.

Containerd ctr privilege escalation (PE 2): running a privileged container with --privileged and --net-host flags via the ctr CLI to obtain elevated capabilities and then escaping the container using privileged container escape techniques to achieve host-level access.

Linux privilege escalation C payloads: shell-spawning programs using setresuid/setuid to set effective UID to root or a target user before executing /bin/sh or /bin/bash. Covers three variants including SUID context exploitation and targeted UID escalation to user 1000 via setresuid and execve.

Library hijacking for privilege escalation: overwriting a shared library (e.g., libaudit.so.1) used by a SUID binary (/bin/su) to inject a malicious constructor function that calls setuid(0)/setgid(0) and spawns a root shell. Covers ldd to identify library dependencies and objdump -T to enumerate required symbols for the fake library.

RunC privilege escalation technique: abusing a host-accessible runc binary to generate an OCI container spec (config.json) and add a bind mount of the host root filesystem (src=/, dst=/) with read-write permissions, then running the container to gain full host filesystem access for privilege escalation.

RunC privilege escalation limitations and rootless configuration: caveat that runc runs as root by default so unprivileged execution fails without a rootless configuration, and notes on restrictions inside rootless containers. Describes completing the exploit with runc run demo after preparing the rootfs directory and modified config.json.

Splunk local privilege escalation and persistence: abusing a Splunk instance (port 8090) with known credentials to execute a shell as the Splunk service user or root. Also covers stealing and cracking Splunk password files or adding new credentials when already root, to maintain persistent access.

Splunk Universal Forwarder Agent RCE exploit (PySplunkWhisperer2): using the Splunk API with a known UF agent password to execute arbitrary commands or scripts on all agents in a network, achieving SYSTEM/root access, data exfiltration, and persistence. References exploit-db entries 46238 and 46487 and the SplunkWhisperer2 tool.

SSH Agent Forwarding exploitation technique: discovering ForwardAgent yes in ssh config, hunting SSH_AUTH_SOCK sockets in /tmp and /run/user, and hijacking another user's ssh-agent socket to impersonate them and pivot to remote hosts without knowing their private key password.

Explanation of why SSH agent forwarding hijacking works: SSH_AUTH_SOCK grants access to decrypted in-memory private keys of the agent owner, allowing lateral movement even without the key passphrase. Also covers extracting the raw private key from agent memory as root or the socket owner.

Audio steganography WAV LSB technique: hiding data in the least significant bits of PCM audio samples with minimal perceptible waveform change, supporting 1+ bits per sample, channel interleaving, and stride permutations. Also covers phase coding, echo hiding, spread-spectrum embedding, and codec-side-channel steganography families.

DTMF audio steganography detection technique: decoding hidden data encoded as dual-tone multi-frequency telephone keypad signals in audio files. References online DTMF decoder tools (unframework.github.io/dtmf-detect, dialabc.com) for identifying keypad tone sequences in CTF audio challenges.

macOS MDM / Apple device serial number format overview: 12-character alphanumeric structure where segments encode manufacturing location, year and week of manufacture, unique device identifier, and model number. Useful for device fingerprinting and MDM enrollment analysis.

Apple serial number manufacturing location codes: mapping of the first three characters to specific factories worldwide including USA, Mexico, Ireland, Czech Republic, Singapore, Malaysia, Korea, Taiwan, China, and Refurbished (RM) identifiers. Relevant to MDM device provenance and red team OSINT.

macOS NVRAM security overview: boot-time firmware configuration variables including boot-args for kernel flags, csr-active-config SIP bitmask, and efi-boot-device-data. Covers Apple Silicon Secure Storage Component (SSC) binding and the split between system-protected and non-system NVRAM variables relevant to SIP bypass and AMFI manipulation.

macOS NVRAM references section: links to Apple Platform Security boot process documentation, Apple Security Updates page for NVRAM-related CVEs, and Duo Labs research on Apple T2 XPC security. Serves as a pointer to authoritative sources for macOS firmware and Secure Boot attack surface research.

macOS defensive firewall tools: Little Snitch (per-process outbound connection monitoring with GUI alerting) and LuLu (Objective-See open-source firewall for suspicious connection detection). Both tools are relevant to red team evasion and blue team endpoint monitoring on macOS.

macOS persistence detection tools: KnockKnock (one-shot Objective-See scanner for common malware persistence locations) and BlockBlock (real-time monitoring for processes that establish persistence mechanisms). Essential defensive tooling for detecting macOS malware and red team implants.

macOS LaunchServices database internals: using lsregister and lsdtrip to dump installed application metadata including URL scheme handlers and MIME types. Covers the /usr/libexec/lsd daemon, XPC services it exposes (lsd.open, lsd.openurl), required entitlements for changing default handlers, and querying running apps via lsappinfo.

Querying macOS file extension and URL scheme app handlers: using lsregister dump with grep, SwiftDefaultApps (getSchemes, getApps, getUTIs, getHandler), and reading Info.plist CFBundleTypeExtensions to enumerate which applications handle specific file types and URL protocols. Useful for privilege escalation via handler hijacking research.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1401: Device Administrator Permissions abuse technique. Covers how adversaries request Android device administrator API permissions to perform malicious actions including device lockout (T1446), data deletion (T1447), disabling cameras, and preventing app uninstall. Notes that Input Injection (T1516) can be combined to silently self-grant admin rights.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1402: Broadcast Receivers persistence and execution technique on Android. Covers how malicious apps register for system-wide broadcast intents at runtime to trigger actions on device events (network changes, screen unlock). Describes inter-app intent abuse and Android 8 (API level 26) restrictions on implicit manifest-registered broadcast receivers.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1403: Modify Cached Executable Code defense evasion technique on Android. Covers adversary abuse of Android Runtime (ART) ahead-of-time compiled code cache via escalated privileges to conceal malicious behavior, bypassing integrity checks that protect system partition code.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1404: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation technique on mobile platforms. Covers how adversaries exploit software vulnerabilities in applications, OS components, or the kernel to elevate from unprivileged/user-level to root permissions, circumventing mobile OS permission level security constructions.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1406.002: Software Packing defense evasion sub-technique. Covers use of packers (e.g. FTT) to compress or encrypt mobile executables to alter file signatures and evade signature-based detection, with decompression occurring in-memory at runtime. Applies to mobile malware obfuscation.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1407: Download New Code at Runtime defense evasion technique. Covers how Android and iOS malware downloads and executes dynamic code post-installation to bypass static analysis and app store scans. Android vectors include native code, Dalvik code, and WebView JavascriptInterface; iOS vector includes JSPatch library abuse.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1409: Stored Application Data collection technique. Covers adversary access to sensitive data from installed apps (e.g. Facebook, WeChat, Gmail) via three mobile OS sandbox bypass scenarios: unprotected external storage, insecure internal storage permissions (777), or root access on the device.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1410: Network Traffic Capture or Redirection credential access technique. Covers malicious app registration as VPN client on Android/iOS to intercept packets, OS privilege escalation for traffic access, and redirection via VPN connections or proxy manipulation. Notes Skycure malicious iOS Configuration Profile attack and encryption as a mitigation.

Wi-Fi PCAP analysis: brute-forcing WPA/WPA2 PSK passphrases captured in a pcap file using aircrack-ng with a wordlist targeted at a specific BSSID. Covers identifying authentication handshakes in packet captures and recovering the pre-shared key needed to decrypt subsequent traffic.

Wi-Fi PCAP analysis: discovering unknown MAC addresses transmitting on a wireless network using Wireshark display filter expressions for wlan.ta, wlan.fc.type, and wlan.addr fields. Covers refining filters to exclude known MACs and tracing unknown device traffic via protocol filters (FTP, HTTP, SSH, Telnet) after decryption.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1412: Capture SMS Messages credential access technique. Covers malicious app interception of SMS-based MFA codes and authentication credentials on Android (requiring SMS receive permission) and iOS (requiring privilege escalation). Highlights SMS as a common MFA transport and the permission model differences between platforms.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1413: Access Sensitive Data in Device Logs collection technique. Covers READ_LOGS permission abuse on Android prior to 4.1 to extract private keys, passwords, and credentials from system logs. On Android 4.1+ privilege escalation is required to access device logs.

macOS XPC connecting process security checks: seven-step verification chain covering Apple-signed certificate, team ID, bundle ID, software version, hardened runtime entitlements, service-specific entitlements, and audit token vs PID. Explains PID reuse attack risk and why xpc_dictionary_get_audit_token should replace processIdentifier and xpc_connection_get_audit_token.

XPC shouldAcceptNewConnection implementation examples in Objective-C: secure vs vulnerable process verification using SecRequirementCreateWithString, SecCodeCheckValidity, SecTaskCreateWithAuditToken, and SecTaskValidateForRequirement. Shows code signing flag checks (cs_hard, cs_kill, cs_restrict, cs_require_lv, cs_runtime) to guard against process injection without version pinning.

LFI to RCE via PHP compress.zlib:// stream wrapper and PHP_STREAM_PREFER_STDIO flag. Covers how file_get_contents with compress.zlib:// keeps a connection open and allows the attacker server to write additional data into the same temp file after the initial HTTP response.

LFI to RCE race condition exploit using compress.zlib:// stream and temp file path disclosure. Covers the CTF technique of exfiltrating the temp file path, then exploiting a race condition window to inject PHP payload after the forbidden-character check but before file inclusion execution.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1416 URI Hijacking: adversaries register custom URI schemes to intercept OAuth authorization codes or tokens intended for legitimate apps, enabling credential theft or phishing via SSO redirect interception on Android and iOS.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1417.001 Keylogging: technique for capturing credentials on mobile devices via rogue third-party keyboard apps or Android AccessibilityService abuse (TYPE_VIEW_TEXT_CHANGED events), with additional methods possible on rooted devices.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1417 Input Capture: parent technique covering methods adversaries use to steal credentials or sensitive data from mobile users, including transparent keylogging (T1417.001) and deceptive GUI input capture (T1417.002) on Android and iOS.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1418.001 Security Software Discovery: adversaries enumerate installed mobile security products and configurations on a compromised device to inform follow-on decisions such as whether to proceed with full infection or avoid detection.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1418 Software Discovery: adversaries enumerate installed applications on a mobile device to identify security tools, target apps, or other software that shapes follow-on attack behavior on Android or iOS.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1420 File and Directory Discovery: adversaries enumerate files and directories on mobile devices, constrained by Android SELinux policies and iOS sandboxing without escalated privileges, with external storage typically visible on Android.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1421 System Network Connections Discovery: adversaries query Android APIs (WifiInfo, BluetoothAdapter, TelephonyManager.getAllCellInfo) requiring ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION permission to enumerate Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and cellular network connections on a compromised device.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1422.001 Internet Connection Discovery: adversaries verify internet connectivity on compromised mobile devices (e.g., via adb shell netstat) to confirm C2 reachability and identify proxy servers or redirectors before establishing command-and-control communications.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1422.002 Wi-Fi Discovery: adversaries enumerate Wi-Fi network names and stored passwords on compromised mobile devices to support Discovery or Credential Access activity in ongoing and future campaigns.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1422 System Network Configuration Discovery: adversaries retrieve IP/MAC addresses and network interface details via Android java.net.NetworkInterface or TelephonyManager (IMSI/IMEI pre-Android 10); iOS blocks this without root access; informs lateral movement targeting.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1423: Network Service Scanning. Covers adversary use of port scans and vulnerability scans from mobile devices to enumerate services on remote hosts, including exploiting VPN access to reach internal enterprise networks.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1424: Process Discovery on Android and iOS. Covers adversary enumeration of running processes via ps command, /proc directory (pre-Android 7), hidepid kernel restriction (Android 7+), and sysctl on older iOS versions.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1426: System Information Discovery on Android and iOS. Covers adversary collection of OS version, patch level, and hardware architecture via android.os.Build class on Android and restricted device model/iOS version queries on iOS.

macOS extended attributes (xattr) and ACL manipulation: setting restrictive POSIX ACLs (deny write, writeattr, writeextattr, writesecurity, chown) on files via chmod +a, reading ACL entries with acl_get_file/acl_to_text, and encoding ACL data as hex. Includes get_acls C tool source for dumping extended ACL entries of arbitrary file paths.

macOS setxattr exploitation technique: embedding raw ACL hex blobs into custom extended attributes (com.apple.xxx.xxxx) using setxattr syscall and a C set_xattr tool. Demonstrates creating protected directories where the embedded xattr carries deny ACL data, relevant to sandbox escape and Finder Flags bypass research.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1428: Exploitation of Remote Services for lateral movement. Covers adversary exploitation of vulnerable enterprise servers and workstations via mobile device VPN access, targeting unpatched software to gain unauthorized internal access and achieve privilege escalation.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1430.001: Location Tracking via Remote Device Management Services. Reference links covering LocationSmart carrier location data leak (Krebs 2018) and NIST Mobile Threat Catalogue entries for ecosystem and EMM-based location tracking threats.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1433: Access Call Log. Covers adversary collection of call log data on Android via OS APIs or direct file access with elevated privileges, and the requirement for privilege escalation on iOS where call log access is restricted to applications.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1436: Commonly Used Port for C2 communication. Covers adversary use of standard ports TCP 80 (HTTP), TCP 443 (HTTPS), TCP 25 (SMTP), TCP/UDP 53 (DNS) to blend malicious traffic with normal network activity and bypass firewall or IDS filtering.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1437.001: C2 over Web Protocols (HTTP/HTTPS). Covers adversary abuse of HTTP/HTTPS and mobile push notification services including Google Cloud Messaging (GCM), Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM), and Apple Push Notification Service (APNS) to blend C2 traffic with normal device traffic.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1437: Application Layer Protocol for C2. Covers adversary use of application layer protocols (web browsing, file transfer, email, DNS) to embed commands and results in legitimate-looking traffic to evade network filtering and detection.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1438: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium. Covers adversary data exfiltration via alternative radio channels such as Bluetooth or RF when C2 runs over standard internet, exploiting weaker monitoring of non-enterprise-routed connections.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1439: Eavesdrop on Insecure Network Communication. Covers adversary interception of unencrypted or weakly encrypted network traffic on mobile devices, referencing mHealth Android app security research and NIST Mobile Threat Catalogue entries APP-0 and APP-1 on application-layer network eavesdropping threats.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1447: Delete Device Data. Covers adversary wiping of a mobile device or deletion of individual files to hide activity or manipulate outcomes. Discusses administrator privileges required for full device wipe via Android DevicePolicyManager, and targeted deletion of update files or attacker-specified data for impact.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1448: Carrier Billing Fraud. Covers malicious app abuse of SMS toll fraud and SMS shortcode purchases against victim carrier billing. Explains device-only verification gap exploited by adversaries, toll billing via cellular web endpoints, Android SEND_SMS permission requirement, and Android 4.2+ premium SMS consent mitigations.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1450: Exploit SS7 to Track Device Location. Covers adversary abuse of SS7 (Signaling System 7) telecom protocol weaknesses to track mobile device geolocation. References 3GPP security specifications, FCC CSRIC working group report, Positive Technologies SS7 attack data, and CCC conference research on SS7 locate, track, and manipulate attacks.

ADB (Android Debug Bridge) overview for Android pentesting. Covers connecting to physical and emulated devices over USB or network, copying files, installing/uninstalling apps, executing shell commands, backing up data, and reading logs.

Smali code modification technique for Android pentesting. Covers decompiling an APK, modifying Smali bytecode to access hidden information or bypass checks, and recompiling the APK as an alternative to dynamic analysis hooks.

Miscellaneous Android pentesting tricks index. Lists techniques including Play Store location spoofing, Play Integrity attestation bypass, app-level virtualization abuse, Shizuku privileged API, insecure in-app update RCE, accessibility service abuse, IME abuse, and NFC/EMV HCE relay attacks.

justapk tool for automated multi-source APK acquisition with Cloudflare bypass. Covers the fallback chain across APK20, F-Droid, APKPure, APKMirror, Uptodown, and APKCombo using curl_cffi TLS fingerprint impersonation, plus ADB APK extraction and APKEditor split-APK merging.

Android malware tradecraft: native staging and fileless DEX loaders. Covers droppers that embed native .so libraries to decrypt a second ELF via JNI, then load payload DEX entirely in memory using dalvik.system.InMemoryDexClassLoader. Includes a Frida hook to dump the in-memory DEX buffer.

Android malware persistence technique using foreground service and MediaPlayer audio loop. A ForegroundService with a pinned notification continuously plays a near-inaudible audio clip via MediaPlayer to keep the process alive and prevent OS inactivity kills.

Android banking trojan technique: accessibility overlay combined with ACTION_SET_TEXT hijacking. After accessibility permission is granted, the trojan monitors the foreground app, renders a WebView overlay, and silently replaces transaction fields (e.g., crypto addresses) using AccessibilityNodeInfo.ACTION_SET_TEXT.

Jezail rooted Android pentesting toolkit. Runs on Magisk/rootAVD rooted devices, exposes an HTTP server on tcp/8080 with a Flutter web UI, REST API, and Swagger docs. Covers installation via adb and emulator port-forwarding to access the UI from a host machine.

Android pentesting case studies and vulnerability references index. Links to topics including iOS keyboard remote input injection, Android rooting framework auth bypass with syscall hooks, abusing Android media pipeline image parsers, and firmware-level Zygote backdoor via libandroid_runtime.

Static analysis of Android APKs: searching for sensitive strings. Covers hunting for hardcoded passwords, API keys, URLs, tokens, Bluetooth UUIDs, and backdoors in APK string tables. Also highlights misconfigured Firebase database URL discovery.

Static analysis of AndroidManifest.xml and strings.xml for security vulnerabilities. Covers debuggable flag, allowBackup setting, networkSecurityConfig, exported activities and services, exposed content providers and FileProviders, broadcast receivers, URL schemes, SDK version attributes, and hardcoded secrets in strings.xml.

Tapjacking attack on Android applications. A malicious app positions itself over a victim app to intercept user touch interactions, causing the victim to unknowingly perform actions on the underlying legitimate app.

Android task hijacking vulnerability via launchMode singleTask without taskAffinity. An attacker app launched before the legitimate app can hijack its back-stack task, causing users to interact with the malicious app while believing they are using the real one.

Insecure data storage in Android internal and external storage. Covers risks of MODE_WORLD_READABLE/MODE_WORLD_WRITABLE file permissions, globally accessible external storage (SD card), the need for input validation on externally sourced data, and API 17 scoped storage restrictions.

Insecure data storage: sensitive data in cleartext in shared preferences and SQLite databases. Covers finding plaintext credentials or tokens in /data/data/<packagename>/shared_prefs/ and /data/data/<packagename>/databases/ during Android pentesting.

Broken TLS in Android apps: accepting all certificates. Covers the SSLSocketFactory.ALLOW_ALL_HOSTNAME_VERIFIER misconfiguration that disables hostname verification, and how to test it by intercepting traffic with Burp without a trusted CA on the device.

Broken cryptography in Android apps. Covers poor key management (hardcoded or predictable encryption keys in local storage) and use of deprecated or insecure algorithms such as RC4, MD4, MD5, and SHA1 for authorization checks, data storage, or transmission.

Additional Android static analysis checks for sensitive apps. Covers APK obfuscation, root detection, emulator detection, integrity self-checks, and using APKiD to identify the compiler, packer, or obfuscator used to build an APK.

Superpacked APKs: Meta's proprietary APK compression algorithm. Covers how superpacked apps bundle content into a single compressed file and two approaches for analysis: building a decompressor app or executing the app and harvesting decompressed files from the filesystem.

Automated static code analysis of Android APKs using mariana-trench. The tool scans Dalvik bytecode for data-flow vulnerabilities by mapping user-controlled sources to dangerous sinks via configurable rules, identifying injection and data-leakage vulnerabilities.

Interesting Android API functions to audit during static analysis. Covers code execution sinks (Runtime.exec, ProcessBuilder, system()), SMS-sending APIs, native library loading (System.loadLibrary, System.load), and in-memory JNI shellcode execution via mmap/mprotect.

Online dynamic analysis of Android APKs using Appetize.io. Covers uploading and running APKs in a cloud emulator, viewing application logs in a browser, and connecting via ADB to use Drozer and Frida inside the hosted emulator.

Local dynamic analysis using Android emulators. Covers setup of Android Studio AVD (x86 with ARM library support), Genymotion (VirtualBox-based, supports Frida and Drozer), and Nox (free but no Frida/Drozer support), including Bridge Network mode configuration in Genymotion.

Dynamic analysis on physical Android devices. Covers enabling developer options and USB debugging, recommended workflow using MobSF plus pidcat, and Magisk/Zygisk rooting notes for Pixel devices including DenyList root hiding, LSPosed/Shamiko, OTA recovery, and scrcpy screen mirroring.

Unintended data leakage in Android apps during dynamic analysis. Covers sensitive data exposure via logcat/pidcat debugging logs, clipboard caching accessible by other apps, crash log exfiltration, and analytics data leakage to third-party services like Google Adsense.

Dynamic analysis of SQLite databases in Android apps. Covers locating app databases at /data/data/<packagename>/databases, enumerating tables and schema with .tables and .schema, and identifying sensitive cleartext data or weakly encrypted data with an accessible key.

Drozer tool for exploiting Android IPC components. Covers how Drozer impersonates an Android app to interact with exported activities, services, and content providers via Android's IPC mechanism, enabling exploitation without requiring device root.

Exploiting exported Android activities for authorization bypass and sensitive data leakage. Covers invoking exported activities via Drozer or adb am start to bypass authentication, accessing sensitive screens, and exploiting setResult() returning sensitive data from unprotected exported activities.

Exploiting Android content providers via Drozer. Covers extracting sensitive data from exported or improperly protected content providers, and testing for SQL injection and path traversal vulnerabilities in content provider query interfaces.

Exploiting exported Android services with Drozer. Covers auditing services that start with onStartCommand, testing for confidential data extraction, authentication bypass, and other vulnerabilities in services that receive, process, and optionally return data.

Exploiting Android broadcast receivers with Drozer. Covers how broadcast receivers listen for specific message types via onReceive, and how improperly handled messages can lead to exploitable vulnerabilities in the component.

Exploiting Android deep links and custom URL schemes. Covers discovering schemes with MobSF, triggering them via adb am start or browser HTML, finding the onNewIntent handler, testing for sensitive data in URL parameters, path traversal via path parameters, open redirect, account takeover via CSRF-free endpoints, and assetlinks.json misconfigurations.

Transport layer security failures in Android apps. Covers improper certificate validation (accepting self-signed certs), weak SSL/TLS cipher suite negotiation enabling MITM attacks, and mixed-channel leakage where sensitive session data is transmitted over unencrypted HTTP after authenticating over HTTPS.

Android TLS certificate verification testing. Covers verifying server certificate integrity to detect insecure TLS configurations and sensitive data transmitted over unencrypted channels, with guidance on dynamic testing steps.

Android HTTPS traffic inspection via proxy certificate installation. Covers installing a Burp CA certificate on an AVD, modifying Network Security Config for API Level 24+ apps to accept custom CAs, and handling Flutter apps which maintain their own CA trust store independently.

Static detection of SSL/TLS certificate pinning in Android APKs using SSLPinDetect. The tool decompiles APKs via apktool and scans Smali code with regex patterns to locate OkHttp CertificatePinner usage, custom X509TrustManager.checkServerTrusted overrides, SSLContext custom managers, and Network Security Config XML pins.

SSLPinDetect usage, pattern rules, and detection targets for Android SSL pinning analysis. Covers verbose mode output (path:line + snippet), JSON pattern rule extension for OkHttp and TrustManager overrides, multi-threaded scanning, and the smali-sslpin-patterns collection for planning Frida hooks or static patches.

Bypassing Android SSL pinning to inspect HTTPS traffic. Covers four methods: apk-mitm (APK patching without root), Frida with Burp/Genymotion, objection automated ssl pinning disable command, MobSF dynamic analysis, and iptables-based traffic forwarding to Burp.

Frida dynamic instrumentation toolkit for Android pentesting. Covers runtime method hooking to change behavior, extract values, and execute arbitrary code; references the Frida tutorial, RMS Runtime Mobile Security GUI, objection and appmon automation tools, Frida codeshare scripts, and linjector for bypassing anti-Frida ptrace detection.

Android Keystore sensitive data auditing during pentesting. Covers accessing cleartext secrets stored in the Keystore with sufficient privileges, and using the WithSecureLabs tracer-cipher.js Frida script to intercept Keystore cipher operations at runtime.

Background snapshot data leakage in Android apps. Android stores UI snapshots in /data/system_ce/0/snapshots when an app is backgrounded; sensitive data in those snapshots can be stolen by privileged users. Mitigation is setting FLAG_SECURE on the window to prevent screenshot capture.

Android Intent injection vulnerability. Proxy components (activities, services, broadcast receivers) that forward externally supplied Intents via startActivity or sendBroadcast can be abused to trigger non-exported components or access sensitive content providers. WebView URL-to-Intent conversion via Intent.parseUri is a common attack vector.

Intent injection key takeaways. Analogous to web Open Redirect; attackers pass malicious Intent extras to redirect execution to unsafe operations, expose non-exported components and content providers, or exploit WebView URL-to-Intent conversion to trigger unintended actions.

Android client-side injection vulnerabilities. Covers SQL injection in dynamic queries and content providers, JavaScript injection (XSS) via WebView with JS enabled, local file inclusion via WebView filesystem access, eternal session cookies not revoked after logout, and Secure flag misconfiguration in cookies.

MobSF (Mobile Security Framework) static analysis for Android, iOS, and Windows apps. Covers Docker-based deployment, web-based vulnerability assessment UI, ZIP source code analysis, diff/compare reports, and VirusTotal integration for hash or file submission.

MobSF assisted dynamic analysis with Genymotion and Frida. Covers automatic Frida startup, traffic capture, SSL pinning bypass, root and debugger detection bypass, exported activity invocation, Frida Live Logs, Live API Monitor, and auxiliary Frida features including class enumeration, string capture, string comparison tracing, and method tracing.

MobSF dynamic analysis shell commands and HTTP traffic tools. Covers the built-in adb/MobSF shell interface, activity and service enumeration commands, HTTP(S) traffic capture viewer, forwarding captured requests to Burp or OWASP ZAP via HTTPTools, Web API Fuzzer, and resetting misconfigured proxy settings via adb.

Qark (Quick Android Review Kit) automated vulnerability scanner by LinkedIn. Analyzes Android source code or APKs for security issues including exposed activities, intents, and tapjacking; generates proof-of-concept deployable APKs and ADB exploit commands without requiring a rooted device.

ReverseAPK automated Android APK analysis tool. Decompiles APKs to Java and Smali, analyzes AndroidManifest.xml for common vulnerabilities, performs static source code analysis for device info exposure and other security issues, and displays all extracted files for review.

SUPER Android Analyzer command-line APK vulnerability scanner. Decompresses APKs and applies customizable JSON rule sets (rules.json) to detect security vulnerabilities across Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms.

StaCoAn cross-platform static code analysis tool for Android and iOS apps. Accepts drag-and-drop APK or IPA files, generates visual and portable HTML reports, and supports customizable wordlists for bug bounty hunters and security testers.

Androwarn static analysis tool for detecting malicious Android app behaviors. Uses androguard to analyze Dalvik bytecode (Smali) and identifies telephony identifier exfiltration, audio/video interception, PIM data modification, and arbitrary code execution patterns.

MARA Framework (Mobile Application Reverse Engineering and Analysis Framework). Integrates smalisca, ClassyShark, androbugs, androwarn, and APKiD for APK analysis; extracts Java/Smali code, private data via regex, manifest details, domain TLS posture via testssl/pyssltest, and supports deobfuscation via apk-deguard.

ProGuard Java obfuscation tool for Android APKs. Open-source command-line tool bundled with the Android SDK that shrinks, optimizes, and obfuscates Java bytecode by removing unused instructions; runs automatically during release builds.

DexGuard APK obfuscation and deobfuscation. Covers DexGuard's runtime operation: loading resources as InputStream, decrypting via FilterInputStream subclass, applying cosmetic obfuscation, extracting a DEX from ZipInputStream, and loading it with loadDex; references a step-by-step deobfuscation guide.

Simplify generic Android deobfuscator. Virtually executes an app to model its behavior and optimizes the bytecode to produce semantically equivalent but more human-readable code, handling arbitrary obfuscation schemes without requiring obfuscation-specific logic.

Android pentesting reference list. Links to OWASP Mobile App Security project, Play Integrity API bypass research, SSLPinDetect tool and smali-sslpin-patterns, Jezail toolkit, justapk downloader, CoRPhone in-memory JNI pipeline, BeatBanker dual-mode Android Trojan analysis, and Android bug bounty lab setup guides.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1453: Abuse Accessibility Features. Covers adversary misuse of Android accessibility APIs to steal credentials and spread malware. Describes overlay phishing attacks mimicking login screens and accessibility-based keylogging of EditText fields, referencing FluBot malware. Related to T1417/001 Keylogging sub-technique.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1456: Drive-By Compromise. Covers adversary exploitation of mobile or desktop web browsers by luring victims to attacker-controlled or compromised websites. Describes malicious JavaScript/iFrame injection, malvertising, watering hole attacks targeting specific communities, and the four-step drive-by exploit delivery process including browser version fingerprinting.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1463: Manipulate Device Communication. Covers adversary-in-the-middle attacks against mobile apps with weak or misconfigured TLS, enabling undetected manipulation of network traffic. References FireEye 2014 research finding 68% of top 1,000 free Google Play apps had at least one TLS implementation vulnerability.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1465: Rogue Wi-Fi Access Points. Covers adversary deployment of fraudulent wireless access points to intercept mobile device traffic. References Kaspersky DarkHotel APT campaign, NIST SP 800-153 wireless security guidelines, and NIST Mobile Threat Catalogue LPN-0 LAN/PAN threat entry.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1466: Downgrade to Insecure Protocols. Covers adversary-forced protocol downgrade on mobile devices by jamming LTE frequencies to force fallback to weaker protocols such as GSM, making communications easier to eavesdrop or manipulate. References NIST SP 800-187 on LTE network security.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1467: Rogue Cellular Base Station. Covers adversary use of fake cell towers (IMSI catchers / femtocells) to intercept mobile phone calls and data. References Computerworld research on femtocell exploitation and NIST Mobile Threat Catalogue CEL-7 cellular infrastructure threat entry.

LFI2RCE via PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS: exploiting the session.upload_progress.enabled PHP setting to force session creation without a prior session, injecting attacker-controlled content into the session file via multipart POST. Race condition against session.upload_progress.cleanup required to include the session file through LFI before cleanup.

LFI2RCE via PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS CTF technique: removing the upload_progress_ prefix by triple base64-encoding the payload then decoding via convert.base64-decode PHP filter chains, so only attacker-controlled content remains at the start of the session file, enabling valid PHP code execution via LFI race condition.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1469: Remotely Wipe Data Without Authorization. Covers adversary-initiated remote wipe of mobile device data via MDM/EMM controls or cloud account access, with references to the Mat Honan Apple/Amazon incident and NIST Mobile Threat Catalogue entries ECO-5 and EMM-7.

Android APK decompilation tools overview: introduction to the decompiler landscape for JARs and APKs with a reference to the 2021 decompilation guide covering tools like CFR, JD-Gui, and Jadx. Starting point for Android reverse engineering and mobile app pentesting toolchain selection.

Jadx APK decompiler usage: GUI mode via jadx-gui and CLI decompilation of APK files with options to specify output directory and suppress resources/source/imports. Recommended tool for cross-platform Android Java decompilation during mobile pentesting.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1471: Data Encrypted for Impact. Describes adversary encryption of files on a mobile device to demand ransom or permanently destroy access, covering mobile ransomware tactics where decryption keys may be withheld or never transmitted.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1481.001: Dead Drop Resolver. Covers C2 technique where adversaries embed encoded C2 infrastructure addresses in legitimate web services (e.g., Google, Twitter) so infected devices resolve C2 indirectly, evading detection via SSL/TLS cover and complicating binary analysis.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1481.002: Bidirectional Communication via Web Service C2. Covers adversary use of legitimate web platforms (forums, social media, dev repositories) to both issue commands to and receive output from compromised systems, leveraging SSL/TLS and trusted-domain cover traffic.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1481.003: One-Way Communication via Web Service C2. Covers adversary use of legitimate web services to push commands to compromised systems without receiving return output on the same channel, routing responses through a separate C2 channel or suppressing them entirely.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1481: Web Service C2 (parent technique). Covers adversary abuse of legitimate external web services (social media, cloud platforms) as C2 relay channels to blend malicious traffic with normal network activity, with SSL/TLS protection and resilience through dynamic infrastructure changes.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1509: Non-Standard Port. Covers adversary network evasion by pairing protocols with unexpected ports (e.g., HTTPS over port 8088 or 587 instead of 443) to bypass port-based firewall filtering and confuse network traffic analysis tools.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1512: Video Capture. Covers adversary collection of video and images via a mobile device's camera using OS APIs, requiring android.permission.CAMERA or iOS NSCameraUsageDescription, with elevated access possible on rooted/jailbroken devices; distinct from screen capture (T1513).

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1517: Access Notifications. Covers adversary interception of OS and application notifications containing sensitive data such as SMS-based OTP/2FA codes, enabling credential theft; also covers notification dismissal to hide activity from the victim.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1520: Domain Generation Algorithms (DGA). Covers adversary use of DGAs to procedurally generate large numbers of C2 domain names, making it difficult for defenders to block or sinkhole C2 channels; also noted for malicious app distribution (reference: Rotexy malware).

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1521.001 — Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography. Covers adversary use of symmetric encryption algorithms (AES, Blowfish, RC4) to conceal C2 traffic on mobile platforms, where the same key encrypts and decrypts traffic to evade protocol-level detection.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1521.002 — Encrypted Channel: Asymmetric Cryptography. Covers adversary use of public key algorithms (RSA, ElGamal, ECDSA) to hide C2 traffic on mobile devices, including hybrid schemes where asymmetric crypto establishes keys for subsequent symmetric sessions (SSL/TLS).

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1521.003 — Encrypted Channel: SSL Pinning. Covers adversary abuse of SSL/TLS certificate pinning (certificate pinning and public key pinning) to shield malicious C2 traffic from interception and MITM inspection, bypassing the device trust store.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1521 — Encrypted Channel (parent technique). Covers the broad tactic of using known encryption algorithms to conceal C2 traffic on mobile devices, noting that even secure implementations may leak keys embedded in malware samples or config files.

Android Google Play Store region bypass technique using VPN location spoofing: steps to install Hotspot Shield VPN, connect to a target country server, force-stop and clear Play Store data to reset region detection, then access geo-restricted applications. Relevant to mobile app acquisition for pentesting purposes.

Caveats and limitations of Play Store VPN-based region spoofing: variability in effectiveness based on VPN reliability, potential performance impact on apps, and terms of service considerations when bypassing regional restrictions. Supplementary notes for Android mobile pentesting and app acquisition workflows.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1532 — Archive Collected Data. Covers adversary use of compression and encryption on data collected from mobile devices before exfiltration, using utilities, programming libraries, or custom algorithms to obfuscate contents and reduce network footprint.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1533 — Data from Local System. Covers adversary collection of sensitive data stored locally on mobile devices (authentication tokens, keyboard cache, Wi-Fi passwords, photos, external storage) requiring escalated privileges, prior to exfiltration on Android and iOS.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1575 — Native API. Covers adversary abuse of Android's Native Development Kit (NDK) and Java Native Interface (JNI) to execute malicious C/C++ code at a lower level than the Android SDK, evading standard analysis of Java-layer behaviors.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1576 — Uninstall Malicious Application. Covers self-removal techniques used by mobile malware: silent uninstall via device owner API, file deletion with root access, and accessibility service abuse to interact with uninstall confirmation dialogs on Android.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1577 — Compromise Application Executable. Covers adversary modification of installed Android apps for persistence, including the Janus vulnerability (CVE-2017-13156) allowing arbitrary bytes in APK/DEX files without breaking signatures, and Agent Smith-style repackaging attacks.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1603 — Scheduled Task/Job. Covers adversary abuse of mobile task scheduling APIs for persistent or recurring code execution: Android WorkManager (built on JobScheduler, GcmNetworkManager, AlarmManager) and iOS NSBackgroundActivityScheduler for repeating or one-time background tasks.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1604 Proxy Through Victim: technique where adversaries turn a compromised Android/iOS device into a SOCKS proxy to mask C2 server IP addresses. Covers use of Android Proxy API and raw sockets to relay traffic and evade IP-based restrictions on banking and social media services.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1605 Command-Line Interface: technique covering adversary use of built-in CLI on Android (via ADB or Java Runtime package) and iOS (via jailbroken shell). Describes privilege escalation through superuser binary on rooted/jailbroken devices to execute commands and modify protected system files.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1617 Hooking: defense evasion technique where adversaries use root frameworks such as Xposed or Magisk to hook mobile OS system APIs and alter return values or data structures. Used to hide malicious artifacts and modify system visibility on Android devices with root access.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1618 User Evasion: defense evasion technique where malicious mobile apps use device motion sensors (accelerometer, gyroscope) to detect user interaction and pause malicious activity while the user is active. Requires no user permissions, making behavior completely transparent to the victim.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1623.001 Unix Shell: execution technique covering adversary abuse of Unix shell on Android and iOS devices for command execution, scripting, and persistence. Covers superuser binary invocation on rooted/jailbroken devices, interactive shell access via C2 or SSH, and shell script use for sequential payload delivery.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1623 Command and Scripting Interpreter: parent execution technique covering adversary abuse of command-line interfaces and scripting environments on mobile platforms. Includes Android Unix shell access via ADB and Java Runtime, and delivery of commands through initial access payloads or C2-linked interactive terminals.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1624.001 Broadcast Receivers: Android persistence technique where malicious apps register broadcast intent receivers to trigger execution on system or application events such as SMS receipt, device boot, or screen unlock. Covers Android 8 API-level 26 changes that restrict implicit manifest-registered broadcast receivers.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1624 Event Triggered Execution: parent persistence technique where adversaries abuse mobile OS event subscription mechanisms—such as SMS receipt or device boot completion—to automatically execute malicious code repeatedly. Covers creation or modification of event triggers pointing to malicious content.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1625.001 System Runtime API Hijacking: Android persistence technique where adversaries overwrite standard OS API libraries with malicious alternatives to hook core functions. Ensures adversary code executes every time the hijacked API function is called by any app on the infected device.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1625 Hijack Execution Flow: parent persistence technique covering adversary manipulation of how mobile operating systems locate and execute programs or libraries. Includes poisoning file directories and intercepting library loading paths to redirect execution to malicious payloads.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1626.001: Device Administrator Permissions abuse on Android. Covers adversary misuse of the Android device administration API to gain elevated control, including password reset, factory reset, camera disabling, and preventing app uninstallation. Notes that Input Injection (T1516) can be chained to silently self-grant admin rights.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1626: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism (parent technique). Describes adversary methods for circumventing native privilege-elevation controls on modern systems to gain higher-level permissions, serving as the parent for sub-techniques such as Device Administrator Permissions abuse on Android.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1627.001: Geofencing as a malware evasion technique on Android and iOS. Covers use of Android Geofencing API with ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION and ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION permissions, iOS requestWhenInUseAuthorization/requestAlwaysAuthorization APIs, and location-based payload gating to evade analysis environments and restrict malicious behavior by geography.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1627: Execution Guardrails (parent technique). Describes adversary use of environment-specific conditions to constrain payload execution to intended targets, reducing collateral damage. Distinguished from System Checks (T1633.001) by requiring a positive target match rather than sandbox absence. Covers location-based and other environmental guardrails on mobile platforms.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1628.002: User Evasion technique on mobile devices. Covers adversary use of device motion sensors (accelerometer, gyroscope) to detect user interaction and suspend malicious activity during active use, allowing malware to persist undetected. No user permissions required for sensor access, making the technique fully transparent to the victim.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1628.003: Conceal Multimedia Files technique on Android. Covers use of the .nomedia file to hide captured pictures, videos, and screenshots from the Gallery app and prevent other applications from indexing a folder, enabling covert exfiltration. Commonly used by stalkerware and spyware.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1628: Hide Artifacts (parent technique). Describes adversary abuse of mobile OS features and developer APIs to conceal artifacts such as application launcher icons, evading detection. Notes dual-use nature of APIs designed for legitimate UI declutter purposes.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1629.001: Prevent Application Removal on Android. Covers abuse of Android device administration API and accessibility APIs (performGlobalAction) to block uninstallation. Details GLOBAL_ACTION_HOME and GLOBAL_ACTION_BACK injection techniques that redirect users away from the uninstall confirmation modal.

SOCKS proxy protocol fundamentals for pentesting: SOCKS5 operation at OSI Layer 5, TCP proxying and UDP ASSOCIATE command, optional authentication, default port 1080, and socks5h DNS-through-proxy behavior to prevent DNS leaks and host fingerprinting. Background for pivot and tunneling techniques.

SOCKS5 proxy enumeration and egress validation techniques: using curl with --socks5-hostname flag for authenticated and unauthenticated proxy testing, chaining with proxychains4 and nmap to verify internal network reach through a discovered SOCKS proxy on port 1080.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1629.003: Disable or Modify Tools on mobile devices. Covers adversary disabling of security software, modification of SELinux configuration, and interference with security scanning tools via device administrator permission abuse or root exploits to alter protected system files.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1629: Impair Defenses (parent technique). Describes adversary modification of victim environment components to hinder or disable defensive mechanisms including anti-virus, audit logging, and activity detection capabilities. Covers both native mobile defenses and supplemental tools installed by users or MDM administrators.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1630.001: Uninstall Malicious Application. Covers adversary techniques for self-removal of malware from mobile devices via device owner API silent uninstallation, root-level file deletion, or accessibility service abuse to confirm uninstall dialogs on Android.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1630.002: File Deletion. Covers adversary use of mobile device administrator privileges or per-file permissions to delete or wipe data (Office files, databases, emails, custom formats) to hide activity or manipulate outcomes, referencing Android DevicePolicyManager API.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1630: Indicator Removal on Host (parent technique). Covers adversary deletion, alteration, or hiding of artifacts on mobile devices — files, jailbreak status, or the malicious app itself — to evade event collection and mobile security detection.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1631: Process Injection. Covers injecting arbitrary code into a live process address space on Android or iOS to evade defenses and escalate privileges. Notes that legitimate process injection APIs are absent on both platforms; exploitation requires root access or a vulnerability.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1632.001: Code Signing Policy Modification. Covers adversary tampering with mobile code signing enforcement to allow unsigned or unofficially signed apps to execute, using input injection or malicious configuration profiles to bypass Android and iOS signing controls.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1632: Subvert Trust Controls (parent technique). Covers adversary methods to undermine mobile OS and security-product trust mechanisms, including code signing certificates, untrusted-source prompts, and site-trust indicators, enabling execution of unverified applications.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1633.001: System Checks for sandbox/VM evasion. Covers mobile malware techniques to detect analysis environments via host/domain name, network traffic samples, network adapter addresses, CPU core count, memory/drive size, and hardware sensor presence such as motion sensors.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1633: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (parent technique). Covers mobile malware detecting virtual machine environments or sandboxes by checking system artifacts or legitimate user activity, then altering behavior or withholding payloads to avoid analysis.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1634: Credentials from Password Store. Covers adversary access to mobile password storage locations — OS keychains, app-managed stores, and password manager applications — to harvest credentials for lateral movement and access to restricted resources.

Pentesting Distcc on port 3632: overview of the distcc distributed compilation daemon, how it works by offloading compile tasks to remote hosts running distccd, and its default TCP port used for network-based build distribution.

Distcc exploitation resources: Metasploit module exploit/unix/misc/distcc_exec for remote code execution via the distccd daemon on port 3632, with links to Rapid7 module documentation and a GitHub gist for manual exploitation.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1636.001: Calendar Entries collection. Covers adversary use of Android Calendar Content Provider and iOS EventKit framework to exfiltrate calendar data, with a note that jailbroken or rooted devices allow access without user approval.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1636.002 (Call Log): describes how adversaries collect call log data on Android using the Call Log Content Provider, and on rooted/jailbroken devices without user consent. iOS has no standard API for this access.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1636.003 (Contact List): describes how adversaries harvest contact list data using Android's Contacts Content Provider or iOS Contacts framework, and how rooted/jailbroken devices allow access without user approval.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1636.004 (SMS Messages): covers adversary collection of SMS messages via Android's SMS Content Provider. iOS offers no standard API for SMS access; rooted or jailbroken devices may bypass these restrictions entirely.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1636.005 (Accounts): describes adversary enumeration of device accounts using Android AccountManager API (getAccounts() method) or iOS Keychain services, including bypass on rooted/jailbroken devices.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1636 (Protected User Data): parent technique covering adversary abuse of permission-backed OS data stores (calendar, contacts, etc.) on Android and iOS, including manifest/Info.plist permission declarations and bypass via rooted/jailbroken devices.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1637.001 (Domain Generation Algorithms): covers DGA use in mobile malware to procedurally generate C2 domain names, evading blocking and takedowns. References the Rotexy banking trojan as a real-world example.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1637 (Dynamic Resolution): parent technique describing mobile malware dynamically computing C2 infrastructure parameters (domain, IP, port) via shared algorithms to evade detection and remediation.

Pentesting BACnet on UDP port 47808: protocol overview for Building Automation and Control Networks (BACnet), covering ASHRAE/ANSI/ISO 16484-5 standards, use in HVAC, lighting, access control, and fire detection systems, and default port identification.

BACnet device enumeration using Python BAC0 library: manual technique to discover and query BACnet devices on a subnet using BAC0.connect(), whois() broadcast, and readMultiple() to extract device IDs, IPs, company names, model names, and firmware versions.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1639.001 (Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol): describes data theft via unencrypted protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS) separate from the C2 channel, using encoding schemes like base64 or protocol header embedding to obfuscate exfiltrated data.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1639 (Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol): parent technique covering data theft via alternate network protocols (FTP, SMTP, HTTP/S, DNS, SMB, cloud storage) distinct from the primary C2 channel, optionally with encryption or obfuscation.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1641.001 (Transmitted Data Manipulation): covers in-transit data tampering on mobile devices, specifically Android clipboard hijacking via ClipboardManager.OnPrimaryClipChangedListener to swap cryptocurrency wallet addresses. References the Android/Clipper.C trojan distributed via Google Play Store.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1641: Data Manipulation technique. Covers adversary insertion, deletion, or alteration of data on mobile devices to manipulate business outcomes, hide activity, or affect organizational decision-making. Applicable to complex systems requiring specialized expertise.

Pentesting Cisco Smart Install on TCP port 4786: protocol overview describing the Cisco Smart Install feature for automated device configuration and OS image loading, enabled by default on Cisco hardware.

CVE-2018-0171 exploitation via SIET (Smart Install Exploitation Tool): critical CVSS 9.8 buffer overflow in Cisco Smart Install on TCP/4786 enabling RCE, forced reboot, and configuration exfiltration from Cisco Catalyst switches using siet.py -g flag.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1643: Generate Traffic from Victim technique. Covers adversary-controlled outbound traffic generation from compromised mobile devices for carrier billing fraud or app store rating manipulation via SMS (requiring SEND_SMS permission on Android) or general web traffic.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1644: Out of Band Data technique. Covers adversary C2 and exfiltration using non-internet out-of-band channels on mobile devices including SMS, NFC, and Bluetooth. Details Android notification access abuse for reading push/SMS data; notes iOS programmatic restrictions.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1645: Compromise Client Software Binary technique. Covers adversary modification of system software binaries on mobile devices to establish persistence. Includes pre-compiled malicious binary replacement of legitimate system binaries executed by OS or user via adb or terminal emulators.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1655.001: Masquerading sub-technique — Match Legitimate Name or Location. Covers mobile defense evasion by naming malicious apps or packages to mimic trusted applications (e.g., com.google.android.gm), copying legitimate app icons, and placing artifacts in expected locations.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1655: Masquerading parent technique. Covers manipulation of artifact name, location, appearance, or metadata on mobile devices to evade defenses and deceive users or security tools. Includes file type spoofing, legitimate task/service name abuse, and renaming system utilities.

Pentesting Line Printer Daemon (LPD) on port 515/tcp: protocol history from Berkeley Unix and RFC1179, lpr command interaction, control file and data file structure, LPRng implementation, and attack surface via malicious PostScript or PJL print jobs.

PRET tool for LPD printer exploitation: lpdprint and lpdtest utilities enabling interaction with LPD-compatible printers, including file download, upload, deletion, and arbitrary data printing against port 515/tcp targets.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1660: Phishing technique for mobile initial access. Covers smishing (SMS), quishing (QR codes), and vishing (phone calls) as mobile-specific phishing vectors. Discusses spearphishing, social engineering via impersonation, malicious attachments/links, and desktop-to-mobile pivoting via QR codes.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1661: Application Versioning technique. Covers adversary supply chain attack of pushing malicious updates to previously benign apps in Google Play Store or Apple App Store, or via compromised developer accounts, to weaponize an established trusted userbase with acquired permissions.

Pentesting Kibana on TCP port 5601: authentication mechanism tied to Elasticsearch credentials, credential discovery in /etc/kibana/kibana.yml, kibana_system user privilege restrictions, and implications of disabled Elasticsearch authentication for unauthenticated Kibana access.

Post-access actions in Kibana pentesting: Elasticsearch data exploration, user/role/API key management via Stack Management, and version-specific RCE vulnerability check for Kibana versions prior to 6.6.0 in the ELK stack.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1663: Remote Access Software technique. Covers adversary use of legitimate RAT/remote control tools (VNC, TeamViewer, AirDroid, AirMirror) on compromised mobile devices for interactive C2, redundant access channels, reverse connections to attacker infrastructure, and persistence.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1664: Exploitation for Initial Access technique. Covers mobile OS and application vulnerability exploitation for initial device compromise, including zero-click exploits and named exploits FORCEDENTRY, StageFright, and BlueBorne targeting apps, services, OS, and kernel layers.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1670 covering adversary abuse of Android virtualization solutions (e.g., Android Virtualization Framework/AVF) to escape application sandboxes, evade detection, and covertly capture credentials by mimicking legitimate banking apps inside a virtual environment.

MITRE ATT&CK Mobile technique T1676 describing adversary abuse of the linked devices feature in Signal and WhatsApp via malicious QR code phishing to register an attacker-controlled device, enabling persistence, message collection, and contact harvesting on end-to-end encrypted messaging platforms.

Pentesting TFTP on UDP port 69: protocol overview of Trivial File Transfer Protocol per RFC 1350, unauthenticated file transfer design, common use cases for distributing configuration files and ROM images to VoIP handsets and internal network devices.

TFTP file download and upload enumeration techniques: using Metasploit auxiliary module auxiliary/admin/tftp/tftp_transfer_util and Python tftpy library to test unauthenticated read/write access on TFTP servers at UDP port 69.

Pentesting Splunkd on port 8089: vulnerability vectors including unauthenticated free-version access after 60-day trial expiry, default credential weaknesses (admin:changeme), and multiple RCE vectors via Django apps, REST endpoints, scripted inputs, and alerting scripts on Windows and Linux.

Splunk RCE via malicious custom application: technique to achieve remote code execution by deploying a crafted Splunk app package with inputs.conf enabling Python, Bash, or PowerShell reverse shell scripts on both Linux and Windows, using the reverse_shell_splunk framework.

Pentesting Bitcoin node services: port assignments for Bitcoin P2P protocol across mainnet (8333), testnet (18333), signet (38333), and regtest (18444) networks, used for node-to-node communication identification during network reconnaissance.

Bitcoin node enumeration using Nmap scripts: bitcoin-info and bitcoin-getaddr NSE scripts to extract node metadata including network type, version, node ID, last block height, user agent string, and peer address lists from Bitcoin nodes on port 8333.
